counts.facts and the check FAILS". fisc-gxa.2 changes exactly that grouping, so
counts-reconcile and the check package's netCells must be reworked in the same
commit.

GOOD NEWS, MEASURED RATHER THAN ASSUMED: a declared unprojectedScopes entry is
CLEAN under --strict. factsAreProjected returns findings: nil with
subjects == len(s.Facts) when every unprojected fact is declared, so it PASSes,
and --strict only adds a failure on Counts.Vacuous > 0. The ~924 declared facts
fisc-u2v's decision creates are not what would keep the gate red. StatusError is.

CONSEQUENCE: "fisc verify --strict as the CI gate" is not reachable from the two
coverage lanes. It needs fisc-o15's Go half, fisc-9gh, fisc-aes, fisc-gkv and a
counts-reconcile rework. ci.yml:259-264's reason for not passing --strict stands
and should not be deleted on the schedule the original table implied.
close_reason:
Both gates run by hand at f67d300; both clean.

FACTS REBUILD: ./bin/fisc build --output bin/facts-rebuilt.jsonl then cmp against the committed file -- BYTE-IDENTICAL. 240 facts, 5 rules over 10 parts, 4 of 10 parts tying to a printed total covering 24 columns. The six UNCHECKED parts are the transfers and fund-balance blocks, which declare no total_row; that is fisc-mq4's known shape, reported rather than hidden (pkg/cmd/build/report.go exists for exactly this).

FISC VERIFY: exit 0. 19 passed, 0 failed, 5 vacuous, 1 skipped, 0 errored. The skip is source-pdfs-match-both-records, which needs --full.

THE FIVE VACUOUS CHECKS, named so the number is not just a number: fact-departments-resolve (no fact carries a department -- fisc-o15/fisc-5gk.2), fact-funds-resolve (the spine's columns are fund groups, no per-fund column -- fisc-5gk.1), transfer-legs-pair (no link carries a transfer_id -- fisc-4rh), aggregation-invariance (no node carries a parent -- fisc-gxa.2), constraint-tier-vocabulary (no node carries a constraint_tier). Every one of the five is retired by a bead already in the graph, and four of the five by the two coverage lanes. ci.yml deliberately does not pass --strict for this reason.

Incidental confirmation for fisc-kwq: verify reports 'facts-are-projected 240 facts, all of them in one of 2 projections' and prints FY2027's headline (external $226,310,381 vs naive $325,241,780), so the second year really is built and checked today and only the export is pinned.

title: No README, no make site target, and three unfilled CLAUDE.md stubs
description:
There is no README.md in this repository at all. With no git remote and no Pages
deploy, a reader's only orientation is the source tree, and docs/agents/ is
written for agents rather than for a person wondering what this is.

Also missing: a make target that builds the site. The Makefile references dist
only in `clean`. The serve hint (python3 -m http.server -d dist 8000) exists in
site/app.js's file:// branch and nowhere a human would look for it.

Also: CLAUDE.md still carries THREE unfilled template stubs from bd init --
line 83 "_Add your build and test commands here_", line 93 "_Add a brief overview
of your project architecture_", line 97 "_Add your project-specific conventions
here_". AGENTS.md does not have them.

WANTED
- README.md: what this is, what is covered (2 pages of 786 today, and say so),
  what the provenance claim means, how to build and look at it.
- `make site` wrapping fisc export only, plus the serve hint.
- Fill or delete CLAUDE.md's three stubs.

Found in peer review of the landing plan, 2026-08-18.
acceptance_criteria: README.md exists and states current coverage honestly; make site builds the site; CLAUDE.md has no template stubs left
close_reason:
README.md written (126 lines), make site added, all three CLAUDE.md stubs filled.

The README leads with current coverage rather than burying it: a table showing 2 pages mapped of 786, and an explicit 'everything below the fund-group level is not yet mapped'. It states the two things a newcomer would otherwise discover the hard way -- there is no git remote so nothing is deployed and CI has never run, and the extracted-page citations point at a GitHub URL that does not resolve (fisc-ze7).

make site wraps 'fisc export --clean' and echoes the serve hint, which previously existed only in site/app.js's file:// branch. Its comment records that fisc export does not re-run the mapping engine, so the target cannot change a published figure. Running it also regenerated dist/ at HEAD, which retired the .md/.txt staleness: dist/app.js now requests p0066.txt and the built page cites it. dist/ is 388 KB.

CLAUDE.md's three sections now carry the real make targets (including the build --output + cmp form rather than rebuilding facts.jsonl in place), the pipeline in one line, and the four invariants with the TestLeadingMinusIsReallyPositive example. AGENTS.md had no stubs.

make pre-commit green.

title: StatedTotals reads its totals positionally while the data rows are band-placed
description:
After fisc-yqv.2 a part's DATA rows are checked against the page's column bands
while its STATED TOTALS are still found by amountRun (resolve.go), which takes
the first maximal run of exactly n consecutive parsable amounts on the anchor's
line. Two different column models for two halves of the same check.

On a dense page they agree, which is why all 24 spine columns still tie. On the
first sparse page they cannot: a totals row with a hole yields fewer than n
amounts and the run is unfindable, and worse, a mis-columned read could be tied
against a mis-columned total and pass.

Cheap hardening already done: nothing yet, but note amountRun calls tokens(s, 0),
whose offsets are valid keys in the absolute-offset pairing map and alias the top
of the page. Nothing looks up through it today. If StatedTotals starts consulting
the pairing, give amountRun a base and pass `from` first.
acceptance_criteria: a part's stated totals are read by the same column model as its data rows, or the bead records why they cannot be
notes: 2026-08-18 NOT ON THE CRITICAL PATH for the current coverage scope, measured. This bead's trigger is 'the first sparse page' -- a totals row with a hole yielding fewer than n amounts. No page in pp.127-140 or pp.167-170 is sparse: all 18 carry exactly 4 value tokens per data row (see fisc-bau's note of the same date). StatedTotals and the data rows therefore still agree on this scope, as they do on the spine. The two-column-models problem is real and stays open; it just is not blocking. Same reason for the note as fisc-bau's.

title: check.Load should take an fs.FS, not a root path
description:
internal/check.Load takes a Root string and does four things with it: os.DirFS(root), os.DirFS(filepath.Join(root, data)), os.ReadDir over data/extracted, and corpus.OpenDoc(root, id). All four have in-tree fs equivalents -- the FS itself, fs.Sub, fs.ReadDir, and fs.Sub plus corpus.Open(fs.FS), which already exists and is what OpenDoc wraps. Subject.Root is referenced by nothing outside subject.go except one wiring assertion in verify_test.go, so the change is contained.

Two payoffs, the second worth more than the first.

(1) Test cost. repoWithoutPDFs copies all 1575 files / 11.4MB of data/extracted per invocation and runs 32 times (24 call sites, four of them inside table loops, plus five reaching it through repoWithPDFs), serially -- no t.Parallel anywhere in the package. Measured at ~131ms per copy, so ~4.2s of the package's 4.5s non-race runtime is copying, and -race is 10.3s against ~1.2s for every other package. It scales linearly with data/extracted, which is 11.4MB at roughly 10 percent mapping coverage, so fisc-5gk.1 and .2 make it worse.

The copy has to be COMPLETE, which is not the same as having to be re-made 32 times: artifacts-match-manifest hashes every file the manifest lists AND reports every file it does not, so a partial tree is not a repository verify passes over.

(2) The mutation tests get STRONGER. With an fs.FS the failure fixtures become a small overlay over os.DirFS(repoRoot) -- the base is then the real committed corpus rather than a copy of it, so a test cannot pass because the copy diverged from what ships.

Do NOT reach for hardlinks as a shortcut: copyRepoFile and writeRepoFile use os.WriteFile, which is O_TRUNC and would write through a hardlink into the real repository.

Found in peer review of fisc-1wr.5.
acceptance_criteria: check.Load takes an fs.FS; the mutation tests are an overlay over the real committed corpus rather than a copy; internal/check's -race runtime is in line with the other packages; no test writes into the real repository
notes: 2026-08-18 CORRECTION, from peer review of the landing plan. This bead's stated motivation is wrong in one respect: 'It scales linearly with data/extracted, which is 11.4MB at roughly 10 percent mapping coverage, so fisc-5gk.1 and .2 make it worse.' data/extracted/ already holds ALL 786 pages of all three documents -- it is written by tools/extract.py, not by mapping -- so its size does not grow when coverage grows. Mapping more pages adds facts, not artifacts. The test-runtime argument stands on its own merits; the growth argument does not. Not a prerequisite for the coverage lanes.

title: A $-glued figure split across a space reads as a plausible wrong value, and splitDigits cannot see it
description:
CIP p29 prints a project cost as '$21130 083' -- one printed figure of $21,130,083 that pdftotext -layout emits as TWO whitespace-delimited tokens. tokens() yields ['$21130', '083'], amount.Parse('$21130') returns $21,130.00, and a labelled read taking N tokens files that as a value and consumes the '083' as the next column.

This is the fisc-c00 / amounts-fail-closed shape: a plausible wrong value, not an error. internal/amount's splitDigits guard (amount.go:112, 211-215) exists for exactly this artifact -- its doc cites 'a digit-splitting artifact turns 240,000 into 2 40,000' -- but the guard is a regex over ONE token, and here the split falls across a token boundary the guard cannot see.

Found while reviewing the reverted fisc-yun join, which had the same root cause from a different direction (see that bead's notes). Corpus-wide this exact shape ($-glued figure, single space, bare 3-digit group) occurs ONCE, on CIP p29 -- so it is rare, not systemic, and no page in the current PoC scope has it.

Likely already fixed by fisc-yqv.2: with geometry the two tokens have right edges inside the SAME column band, and the substrate-agreement check (the -layout token count for a row must equal the count of geometry words in the column bands) sees 2 where the grid has 1 and fails closed naming the row. Verify that when fisc-yqv.2 lands rather than writing a second guard; if it does hold, close this bead citing the test.
acceptance_criteria: a rule over CIP p29 either reads $21,130,083 correctly or fails closed naming the cell; no path files $21,130 as the value of a printed $21,130,083
close_reason: Caught by fisc-yqv.2's column guard; TestCIPp29SplitFigureFailsClosed carries it. The bead's own hypothesis was wrong -- geometry holds TWO words for '$21130 083' and the substrates agree on every count; what catches it is that both right edges fall in band 0. Conditional on the part declaring column_headers, which every published part does and the parser now enforces per page. See the notes.

title: Re-run the dataviz CVD validator over the tier-0/3/4 touching pairs
description:
FUND_ORDER in site/app.js is a MEASURED result: all 720 orderings of the six fund-group hues were enumerated against the CVD validator, and the chosen order (internal-service, capital, general, special-revenue, enterprise, debt-service) has worst-case CVD deltaE 9.1 light / 8.4 dark. That measurement is over a chart whose middle column is FUND GROUPS.

After fisc-gxa.2 the default General Fund view renders tiers 0, 3, 4 -- the middle column is FUNDS, and tier-4 department nodes are new. Different nodes touch, so the measurement no longer applies to the rendered chart.

Plan is to keep hue keyed by fund group and let a fund node inherit its group's via node.parent, which keeps the palette at six categorical slots. That is a hypothesis, not a result. Re-run the validator over the pairs that actually touch in the new layout and record the numbers here.

Filed because fisc-gxa.2's plan says 'not free; do not pretend it is' -- and without an id, it becomes free.
acceptance_criteria: worst-case CVD deltaE recorded here for light and dark at the new touching pairs; if it drops below the standard this project already met, the ordering or the inheritance rule changes rather than the standard

title: The 'extracted page text is in Git LFS' claim is false, and it is in four places
description:
`.gitattributes` has exactly two lines and puts ONLY data/pdf/** in LFS (67MB, 3 files). data/extracted/ is ordinary git -- 1575 tracked files, 15MB; `git check-attr filter` on a page returns 'unspecified'. But four places assert otherwise:

- site/app.js:263-266 -- says the page text is stored with Git LFS and raw.githubusercontent.com would serve a pointer file.
- internal/export/export.go:57-59 -- says 'the PDFs and their extracted artifacts are stored with Git LFS'.
- internal/export/export_test.go:203-206 and the test NAME TestPageCitesThePDFPageAndNeverTheLFSPointer.
- fisc-gxa.5's own description, which also still says 'the committed pages/pNNNN.md' -- .md is wrong post-fisc-yqv, the artifacts are .txt.

The CONCLUSION each one draws (link the github.com blob view, never raw) is still correct, but for a different reason: corpus.PagePath's doc comment already gives it -- GitHub's blob view renders markdown and collapses the runs of spaces that ARE the column grid.

Why it matters beyond tidiness: the belief this plants is exactly the belief that makes someone set `lfs: true` in a CI workflow. GitHub's free tier is 1GB/month and each LFS checkout here is ~70MB, so ~14 runs exhaust it. Leaving it in the tracker leaves it where the next session looks.
acceptance_criteria: all four statements corrected, each citing the real reason (markdown collapses the grid; the PDFs alone are LFS); the test is renamed to say what it actually asserts; no code behaviour changes
close_reason: Corrected in all four places: site/app.js, internal/export/export.go, internal/export/export_test.go (comment plus the test renamed to TestPageCitesThePDFPageAndTheBlobViewOfTheExtractedPage), and fisc-gxa.5's description. Peer review caught that the test comment initially omitted the .txt/column-grid half of the reason; added.

title: manifest.errors is recorded but no consumer reads it
description:
tools/extract.py records extraction errors in manifest.json rather than only logging them, on the principle that a partial extraction writing a clean-looking manifest defeats the manifest's purpose. But nothing reads them: internal/corpus's manifest struct has no Errors field, and fisc verify does not exist yet.

Consequence: a run that failed on page 5 produces a manifest whose artifact list simply lacks page 5, and Page(5) then returns ErrNotFound -- which corpus.go:41 documents as the NORMAL 'document has no such page' case. Fail-open, same shape as the schema_version finding.

Belongs with fisc-1wr.5 (structural checks) or as its own tier-1 check: a manifest with a non-empty errors list must fail verify loudly. Also nothing enforces the recorded poppler_version.

Found in peer review of fisc-yqv.3.
notes:
2026-08-17 ADDRESSED in lane A4 (fisc-1wr.5), pulled in by peer review of that lane; uncommitted in the main tree and NOT closed by the agent.

manifest.errors now has a consumer: check 'extractor-reported-no-errors' (tier 0) fails when any manifest records a failure, naming stage, page and message per entry (capped at 5) and telling the reader to re-run make extract. internal/corpus decodes errors, warnings and blank_page_count and exposes Errors()/Warnings()/BlankPageCount() -- all three were previously dropped by the reader, which is why nothing could read them.

Warnings deliberately do NOT fail: all three committed extractions carry some (8 in total), poppler exits 0 for a damaged xref and an unread metadata key alike, and a check that failed on them would be red from the day it landed. They are counted into the passing summary instead, with the blank page count -- 'reading the warnings is the human's job' needs the numbers to be in front of the human.

The other half of this bead ('nothing enforces the recorded poppler_version') is also done: check 'extraction-toolchain-pinned' compares extractor_version and poppler_version against corpus.PinnedExtractorVersion/PinnedPopplerVersion.

Review also found the fail-open case that errors alone does NOT catch, and extract.py itself warns about it ('a run whose errors is empty is NOT a promise that every page came out whole'): delete every artifact of an extraction from the directory AND from its manifest and the hash sweep passes, because a bijection between the map and the disk says nothing about size -- 1572 artifacts becomes 1182 and the report still says PASS. Closed by a second, independent check, 'extraction-emitted-every-page': page_count vs one pages/ and one geometry/ artifact per page, in both directions, with each document's page count printed in the passing summary so an emptied extraction cannot hide in an aggregate. page_count is itself checked against sources.yaml's hand-written 'pages:', and registry.LoadSources now refuses a source with pages <= 0, which closes the laundering path of zeroing both.

Verified by transcript: emptying the ACFR extraction from disk and manifest exits 3 on extraction-emitted-every-page while artifacts-match-manifest still passes; a synthetic manifest.errors entry exits 3 on extractor-reported-no-errors while extraction-emitted-every-page still passes. Neither witness subsumes the other.
close_reason: internal/corpus now decodes errors, warnings and blank_page_count (it decoded none of them, which is why nothing could read them), and internal/check has extractor-reported-no-errors: a manifest recording an extraction failure fails the run, naming stage/page/message. Warnings are deliberately not failures -- all three documents carry some and poppler exits 0 for a damaged xref and an unread metadata key alike -- but they and the blank-page count are printed in the passing summary, because decoding them and saying nothing is how reading them becomes nobody's job. Found to still be open during peer review of fisc-1wr.5, where it turned out to be the completeness witness the structural tier was missing rather than a nicety.

title: docs/m0-spike.md rests on premises the extractor replacement deleted
description:
docs/agents/README.md names m0-spike.md as required reading before any non-trivial change, so stale premises there actively mislead. Lines 25-29, 54, 57, 65-70, 73-74 describe: the table substrate and its 46/62/52 percent recall figures, EXTRACTOR_VERSION = 2 and the strip_repeating_text fix, markdown backslash-dash escapes as a seventh corruption mode, and xberg extraction timings.

After fisc-yqv there are no tables, no markdown, and no xberg. The spike's CONCLUSION survives intact and is more strongly supported than before -- page text is the substrate, tables are a trap -- but its evidence needs restating against poppler. The fisc-c00 narrative also needs care: it is still true and still the best worked example in the repo, but strip_repeating_text is now a defect of an extractor the project no longer uses.

Do not delete the document. Restate it.
close_reason:
Annotated rather than rewritten. docs/agents/README.md names this file as required reading, so the stale premises had to be marked in place -- deleting them would have taken finding 4 with them, and finding 4 is the reason the document is kept.

A header note states what changed wholesale (xberg gone, poppler 24.02.0, no table substrate, no markdown, extractor_version 3) and says which findings survive: 2, 3 and 4 intact, 1 and 5 and Cost superseded. Four inline SUPERSEDED blocks:

- Finding 1 (46/62/52 percent table recall): superseded in form, upheld in conclusion. The percentages compare against a substrate fisc-yqv.6 deleted; the conclusion is now structural rather than empirical, and the second substrate that did arrive carries geometry, not content.
- Finding 4 (strip_repeating_text, EXTRACTOR_VERSION = 2): the REMEDY is superseded, the finding is not -- and the note records that fisc-yqv was opened because the same pipeline was later found dropping 33 of 40 rows on p167 and all 13 on p130. The standing lesson is stronger for it.
- Finding 5 (backslash-dash as a seventh corruption mode): superseded outright -- an artefact of markdown output that no longer exists. Added the two shapes found since that are NOT in the original list: a figure split across a token boundary (CIP p29) and printed dashes present in no substrate (CIP p40, fisc-8ln).
- Cost (10 seconds, disable_ocr=True, layout=None): xberg parameters, superseded.

Also settled the Status section: fisc-mq4.7 has closed and internal/mapping publishes 240 facts over 24 columns where the spike read 136 over 16, so the known-good target was hit. Recorded that m0-spike/spike.py no longer runs -- it imports xberg -- and that its output directory holds a dead substrate. Kept as evidence for finding 4, not as anything executable.

Spike-era numbers left as the spike's own, with the real figures given in the header for contrast.

title: A link can never carry a transfer_id
description: fisc-gxa.1 requires paired transfer legs sharing a transfer_id, and fisc-1wr.1 checks that every transfer_id has two equal legs. fact.Fact has no field that could carry one, so internal/project has no input for it and the check is structurally vacuous rather than merely unsatisfied today. Mapping p76 (fisc-5gk.3) will NOT fix this on its own -- the fact model or a link-level convention has to carry the pairing. Raised by the projection implementation.
notes:
2026-08-18 THE ROW SHAPE IS NOW KNOWN, which makes this decidable. p76 prints 22 rows of the form 'Transfer From <source fund> to <destination fund> <4 amounts> <footnote>'. fact.Fact carries a single `fund` field, so one fact cannot hold the pair. The shape that fits the existing model is TWO facts per printed row -- a transfer_out keyed to the source fund and a transfer_in keyed to the destination -- sharing a pairing id and citing the SAME doc_id/page/offset/token, since one printed figure is the provenance for both legs. Note what that does to fact identity: the id tuple (doc_id, rule_id, row_path, row_label, column_path, fiscal_year, basis) would collide for the two legs unless kind or column_path distinguishes them. Decide before fisc-5gk.3.1 authors any YAML. Three of the 22 rows omit the source label because it continues from the row above ('to Wastewater Replacement', 'to 2022 COPS', 'to Downtown LMD'), so the pairing cannot be read off the row label alone.
2026-08-21 DECIDED: TWO FACTS PER PRINTED ROW, AND THE FEARED ID COLLISION DOES
NOT ARISE.

THE SHAPE. p76 prints 22 rows of `Transfer From <source fund> to <dest fund>
<4 amounts> <footnote>`. fact.Fact carries a single Fund, so one fact cannot hold
the pair. Each printed row therefore produces TWO facts:

  - a transfer_out keyed to the SOURCE fund, category transfers/out
  - a transfer_in  keyed to the DESTINATION fund, category transfers/in

both citing the SAME doc_id / page / offset / token, because one printed figure
is the provenance for both legs. That is not a duplication of evidence; it is one
figure being evidence for two directions of one movement.

THE COLLISION THIS BEAD WORRIED ABOUT DOES NOT HAPPEN. Checked against
fact.MakeID (internal/fact/fact.go:127-136). The tuple is
(doc_id, rule_id, row_path, row_label, column_path, fiscal_year, basis). `kind`
is NOT in it -- so the bead is right that kind alone cannot separate the legs.
But the two legs differ on TWO other components already, without any change to
the fact model:

  row_path    -- RowPath (fact.go:143-152) returns the category when no
                 department is present. The out-leg is transfers/out and the
                 in-leg is transfers/in, which are distinct taxonomy slugs.
  column_path -- ColumnPath (fact.go:160-176) emits `fund/<number>`. The
                 out-leg's column is the SOURCE fund, the in-leg's the
                 DESTINATION. Distinct by construction.

So the ids differ twice over, and they differ on the components that carry the
MEANING of the difference rather than on a discriminator bolted on to avoid a
hash clash. NO CHANGE TO MakeID, and no new field on fact.Fact.

WHAT STILL HAS TO BE SOLVED, and it is not identity.

(1) THE PAIRING ID. transfer-legs-pair (internal/check/graph.go:619) checks that
every transfer_id has two equal legs, and Link carries transfer_id in the schema
already. The two legs need a shared value. Since the pair is exactly "the two
facts from one printed figure", the pairing is derivable from the shared
(doc_id, page, offset) -- the legs cite the same token. Prefer deriving it over
storing it: a stored id is a third thing that can be wrong, and this one has a
canonical source. If a stored field is chosen anyway, that is a fact-model change
and needs saying so explicitly.

(2) THREE ROWS OMIT THE SOURCE LABEL because it continues from the row above --
`to Wastewater Replacement`, `to 2022 COPS`, `to Downtown LMD`. So the pairing
CANNOT be read off the row label alone, and neither can the source fund. This is
the same continuation shape as fisc-0cs and fisc-ffy and it is why this bead sits
behind them: the source has to come from the row above, which means the rule has
to be able to SAY that rather than the reader inferring it.

(3) fisc-8dz IS A HARD PREREQUISITE, not an adjacent nicety. The source and
destination are PROSE FUND NAMES in abbreviated form, and five of them are
AMBIGUOUS against data/funds.yaml (Low Income Hsng, Traffic Imp Fee, Host Comm
Impact, Measure D, State Gas Tax each match both an operating fund and a CIP
twin). A leg keyed to the wrong twin is a plausible wrong value that the equal-
legs check would NOT catch, because both legs would still be equal.

WHAT THIS RETIRES. transfer-legs-pair is the fifth and last of the vacuous checks
fisc-0ux enumerates. It is the only one of the five not retired by the two GF
coverage lanes.

WHAT IT DOES NOT RETIRE. The $38,086,737 residual is the CITY'S OWN and mapping
p76 cannot close it -- p76's grand total IS the transfers-in side. fisc-5gk.3
already corrected four places that claimed otherwise. Publishing these facts must
not reintroduce the claim.
close_reason:
Both halves settled, and the second one was the part no bead had.

THE FACT SHAPE was decided in this bead's 2026-08-21 note and is correct: two
facts per printed row, and the feared MakeID collision does not arise because
the legs differ on row_path (transfers/in vs transfers/out) and column_path
(receiving vs paying fund). No field added to fact.Fact, no change to MakeID.
Re-confirmed by TestACounterpartPublishesTheFarLegFromTheSameFigure.

THE MECHANISM did not exist and nothing had checked that. mapping.Resolver
yields one Value per printed token and fact.FromValues built one Fact per Value
-- an unbranched chain with no fan-out anywhere in it, so the decided shape was
unexpressible. c5d11ef adds mapping.Row.Counterpart plus Row.Fund/Row.FundGroup
(the per-row fund dimension fisc-aes (4) identified and left unowned), and makes
FromValues the pipeline's one fan-out point. That placement is deliberate:
CheckTotals sums Values upstream of it, so a counterpart can neither break nor
be caught by a schedule's tie to its own printed total -- proven on the real
page, not asserted.

It also resolves this bead's item (2) for free: the three continuation rows
declare their payer rather than a reader inferring it from the line above.

WHAT THIS BEAD DOES NOT CLOSE, and its title is about that half: a LINK still
cannot carry a transfer_id. internal/project keys cells on
(kind, category, fundGroup) and netCells never reads a fact's fund, so the legs
net into fund-group cells before a pairing could attach. That is fisc-9gh, which
now owns the clause outright; the pairing id is derivable from the shared
(doc_id, page, offset) exactly as this bead preferred, because the two legs now
provably share it by construction.

No facts published: facts.jsonl byte-identical, fisc verify unchanged.

title: fisc build resolves every part twice
description: buildRun calls Resolver.Values for facts and then CheckTotals, which resolves the same part again. Harmless at 10 parts and 240 facts; it is the shape that matters as E7 raises coverage across hundreds of parts. Either have CheckTotals take the values it should check, or cache per (rule, part) in the resolver. Found in code review.
close_reason: Resolver memoizes each part read, error included, keyed on (rule id, page). CheckTotals now returns (*TotalsResult, error) so fisc-2sd is additive, and TotalsResult.Columns fixed a latent disagreement between mappings_test's len(p.Columns) and the build report's non-skip count. Peer review corrected two honesty problems: the doc comment claimed a correctness property the pre-existing page memo already provided, and the test named after the mechanism passed with the mechanism removed. 240 facts and 24 tied columns unmoved; facts.jsonl and the golden byte-identical.

title: internal/registry validates only the fields its consumers read
description: registry.Load's contract is that loading validates, but 'kinds' members are not checked against the five mapping.Kind values, and 'pages', alias terms and contra-row terms are not validated at all. A typo'd kind or a page number outside the document survives load and is discovered, if ever, by a consumer that happens to read it. Found in code review of the initial landing.
notes:
UNBLOCKED by the fisc-ttq correction (2026-08-22). This bead was previously
unlandable as written: it wants `kinds:` members validated against the five
mapping.Kind values at load, and data/taxonomy.yaml declared `kinds: [transfer]`
on all four transfer categories, so registry.Load would have rejected the
committed file. Those four entries now declare transfer_in/transfer_out, and
every `kinds:` member in the file is one of the five. The load-time check can
land without a flag day.

Note it needs mapping.Kind.valid() exported (or a mapping.Kinds() slice) --
it is unexported today, and re-listing the five values inside internal/registry
would be a second spelling of the vocabulary, which the taxonomy header
argues against.
2026-08-22 UNBLOCKED, AND THE HOLE IS CONFIRMED REACHABLE. Two findings.

(1) UNBLOCKED. This bead was previously unlandable in one respect: validating
kinds: members against the five mapping.Kind values would have REJECTED the
committed data/taxonomy.yaml, whose four transfer categories declared
kinds: [transfer] -- a string mapping.Kind has never defined. Commit 6216eda
corrected all four, so every kinds: member in the file is now a real Kind and
the validation can land.

It needs mapping.Kind.valid() exported, or the five values re-listed in
internal/registry. Prefer the export: a second spelling of the vocabulary is
what the taxonomy's own header argues against.

(2) THE HOLE IS REACHABLE TODAY, confirmed by /code-review: setting
transfers/out-to-cip to `kinds: [banana]` leaves fisc verify FULLY GREEN,
because that category carries no facts yet. fact-kind-matches-category compares
a fact's kind against the declared list and a category with no facts is never
consulted, so an invalid kinds: member is invisible until a page that uses the
category is mapped -- possibly years later, and then as a mass failure rather
than as a one-line file error.

That is the same shape as the fisc-ttq bug 6216eda just fixed: two unvalidated
strings agreeing with each other, reported as a pass. The registry is the right
layer -- "a registry that loaded is one whose invariants already hold".

title: Validate rule categories and fund groups against the registries
description: Row.Category and Column.FundGroup are unvalidated free strings in internal/mapping/parse.go. Nothing enforces that a category exists in data/taxonomy.yaml, that an assignable:false rollup slug (taxes, transfers, fund-balance) is refused as a category, or that a fund_group is a real funds.yaml type. fisc verify tier 1 checks this after the fact; the parser should refuse it up front, which is where validate-at-boundaries says it belongs. Depends on internal/registry.

title: Per-row kind override on mapping.Row
description:
The p66-67 spine needs five rules where three would do, because Kind is per-Rule and the transfers and fund-balance rows share a block with the expenditure rows. Each rule therefore re-declares the whole block with skip: true on the rows it does not own -- correct and fail-closed, but verbose and easy to get wrong in review.

Row.Kind as a per-row override of Rule.Kind, exactly as Column.Basis overrides Rule.Basis, would collapse them. NOT done during the first parallel wave because it puts internal/mapping and internal/fact under edit while four agents code against them.

The real cost is bigger than the field: CheckTotals is per-rule and KIND-BLIND. Merging spine-revenues and spine-transfers-in into one rule means the mapped rows no longer sum to TOTAL REVENUES:, so Row.Kind also requires a kind-aware CheckTotals. Do both or neither.
notes:
2026-08-21 NO LONGER OPTIONAL, AND NO LONGER DEFERRABLE PAST fisc-5gk.1. From the
fisc-u2v design pass.

Eleven funds on pp.131-140 print revenue rows AND a Transfers In row inside ONE
printed `Total <fund>`: Stormwater, Wastewater, Wastewater Replacement, Water,
Water Replacement, 2022 COPS, Horizons, Downtown LMD, Workers Comp Insurance,
Facilities Rehab Pgm, and one more.

Rule.Kind is per RULE and CheckTotals is per (rule, part). So without a per-row
override those eleven printed totals CANNOT BE USED AS total_row AT ALL -- not
"are verbose to express", cannot be expressed. The document stops checking our
work on eleven of its own totals, which is the single most valuable check this
project has.

This bead's original framing was cost-only ("five rules where three would do")
and its deferral reason was scheduling ("puts internal/mapping and internal/fact
under edit while four agents code against them"). Both were right at the time.
Neither survives a lane that needs the override to assert a printed total.

The "do both or neither" constraint stands and travels with it: CheckTotals is
KIND-BLIND, so Row.Kind without a kind-aware CheckTotals produces rules whose
mapped rows no longer sum to their declared total. Do not land half.

Precedent for the shape is exact and already in the tree: Column.Basis overrides
Rule.Basis for the same reason ("the column overrides the rule",
internal/fact/fact.go:191-196).

If it is judged too much to land inside fisc-5gk.1, the alternative is to leave
those eleven totals unasserted AND SAY SO IN THE COMMIT -- not to let it pass
unremarked, which is how a missing check becomes invisible.
2026-08-21 THE "DO BOTH OR NEITHER" CONSTRAINT DOES NOT TRANSFER, and reading it
across to fisc-5gk.1 would BREAK the eleven totals this bead was just promoted
to enable. Correcting my own note of earlier today, which said the constraint
"travels with it". It does not.

THE TWO JOBS WANT OPPOSITE THINGS.

This bead's original job: merge spine-revenues (kind revenue,
total_row "TOTAL REVENUES:") with spine-transfers-in. There the printed total
covers ONLY the revenue rows, so a merged rule needs CheckTotals to sum BY KIND
or the mapped rows stop summing to the total.

fisc-5gk.1's job: eleven funds on pp.131-140 print revenue rows AND a
Transfers In row inside ONE printed `Total <fund>`. There the printed total
covers BOTH kinds, and CheckTotals' existing kind-BLINDNESS is exactly what is
wanted.

So "make CheckTotals kind-aware" implemented as "sum only rows whose effective
kind equals the rule's kind" makes p131's Airport block sum to its revenue rows
alone and stop tying to `Total Airport`, which includes Transfers In 3,247,000.
All eleven mixed blocks would fail to build -- the precise outcome the promotion
was meant to prevent.

THE RESOLUTION: the kind filter belongs on the total_row DECLARATION, not on
CheckTotals globally. A total row is the thing that knows which rows it covers,
and saying so is a claim the rule author makes and review can check. That also
matches how this file already works -- Column.Basis overrides Rule.Basis on the
COLUMN, the thing that knows.

WHAT THIS MEANS FOR SEQUENCING. Row.Kind can land with CheckTotals UNCHANGED and
is inert on the existing tree: the only two rules carrying total_row today
(mappings/livermore-budget-fy2026-2027.yaml:143 and :224) are single-kind, so a
kind-aware CheckTotals is a no-op on the spine and the entire risk is in the new
lane. So Row.Kind is safe inside fisc-5gk.1. The spine-rule merge -- the five-
rules-where-three-would-do saving this bead was originally written for -- is
SEPARATE work and should be filed as such rather than bundled.
close_reason:
Row.Kind + Rule.TotalRowKinds land in 8f70ee9. facts.jsonl byte-identical.

THE BEAD'S OWN EXAMPLE WAS WRONG, corrected in the code comment. The 2026-08-21 note says a kind-aware CheckTotals would make 'p131's Airport block stop tying to Total Airport, which includes Transfers In 3,247,000'. Airport prints NO Transfers In at all -- four revenue rows and nothing else. The 3,247,000 is STORMWATER's FY2025-26 transfer, and Total Stormwater 4,416,000 = 1,169,000 charges + 3,247,000 transfers, which is the real worked example and is now the regression test. Same class as the fisc-o15 count corrections: a plausible figure attached to the wrong block.

The 'do both or neither' resolution held exactly as the note predicted. CheckTotals stays kind-blind; the filter is on the total_row DECLARATION (TotalRowKinds), absent by default. The parser refuses every spelling that asserts nothing, including a list naming every kind the rule maps.

The filter's test declares [revenue] on Stormwater -- WRONG about the document -- and asserts the check FAILS naming the revenue-only sum. A filter that could only turn a passing check into another passing check would not be a check.

fisc-56f (the spine merge) is untouched and still P3: it moves rule_id, which is in fact.MakeID's tuple.

title: pkg/cmdutil: atomic writes and output-path safety
description: fisc build and fisc export both need filesystem safety and must not grow two implementations. atomic.go: WriteFile(path, perm, func(io.Writer) error) with the temp file in the SAME directory + fsync + rename (a cross-filesystem rename is a non-atomic copy). path.go: port ResolveOutputDir, SafeCleanDir and WritableDir from ~/repos/solvent-streets/pkg/cmdutil/path.go, where SafeCleanDir refuses to delete a non-empty directory lacking an index.html or marker sentinel so a mistyped --output cannot wipe user data.
close_reason: cmdutil.WriteFile (atomic, temp in same dir) and path.go (ResolveOutputDir/SafeCleanDir/WritableDir) both landed.

title: Vendor d3 and d3-sankey; no npm in the deploy path
description:
PROBLEM: the site needs a Sankey renderer. Every option is a third-party JavaScript dependency, and docs/agents/conventions.md requires a decision bead in the same change for any dependency outside cobra/go-cmp/sqlite/goreleaser (see fisc-j8f for the YAML one).

DECISION: vendor d3@7.9.0 and d3-sankey@0.12.3 as committed minified UMD builds under site/vendor/, with their licenses (both ISC/BSD-3-Clause, both permissive). Fetched ONCE by hand with 'npm pack d3@7.9.0 d3-sankey@0.12.3'.

sha256 of the source tarballs:
  d3-7.9.0.tgz         7e36605710a2ba54846797c8c6d888911341b215ae53257dc32a49a0b824355e
  d3-sankey-0.12.3.tgz 6bd8cdb143d4088ff38179def70954419868d4b95f136c168ffef2dad004ff22
sha256 of the committed files:
  site/vendor/d3.min.js        f2094bbf6141b359722c4fe454eb6c4b0f0e42cc10cc7af921fc158fceb86539
  site/vendor/d3-sankey.min.js 8286db5d6aa049cc6e8a546708943b79dfb4daaefb0ccf42af674ec0ee4c86be

TRADEOFFS: d3.min.js is 280KB, most of which this site does not use; a custom bundle would be smaller but would put a bundler in the build. Vendoring means no dependabot and no automatic CVE alerting -- a d3 CVE is our problem to notice. Accepted because the published site has no third-party runtime dependency, no CDN, and no npm anywhere in the deploy path.

LOAD ORDER: d3-sankey.min.js is UMD and falls back to the global 'd3', so d3.min.js must be loaded first. Verified.

NOTE for re-fetching: cdn.jsdelivr.net is blocked by the proxy in this environment; registry.npmjs.org and github.com are reachable. npm pack works.

npm may appear in a lint-only devDependency (tsc --checkJs on app.js, per fisc-gxa.3, matching solvent-streets) but must never appear in the deploy workflow.
close_reason: d3@7.9.0 and d3-sankey@0.12.3 vendored under site/vendor with licenses and recorded hashes; npm is not in the deploy path.

title: Markdown structure defeats text anchors on the revenue-by-fund family
description:
Two shapes on pp.127-140 and 165-183 that the mq4.2 resolver does not read:

1. Emphasis markers. On p127 stop_at 'Total Property Taxes' leaves trailing text '\n\n**', which the whitespace-only trailing check rejects. The anchor must include the '**' ('**Total Property Taxes'). Works, but it is a trap and nothing documents it.

2. Header tables. 25 pages (grep -l '^| FY 20') put a markdown header table between the section anchor and the first data row, so the 'no digits before the first label' check fires on 'FY 2023-24 | FY 2024-25 | ...'. Fail-closed, but it means pp.131-140 and 165-183 -- the decomposition target -- cannot be mapped as written.

Decide between a header-stripping rule, a carve-out for markdown table rows before the first label, or documenting that these pages need an anchor past the header.
acceptance_criteria: A rule can map p131 without disabling the unmapped-row check; the p127 family's anchor requirements are documented where a rule author will find them.
close_reason: Moot. Its entire subject -- trailing ** emphasis markers and markdown header tables defeating text anchors on pp.127-140/165-183 -- was an artefact of xberg's markdown synthesis. pdftotext -layout emits no markdown, so both shapes are gone. The pages the bead could not map now map. Its second acceptance criterion (document the family's anchor requirements where a rule author will find them) is carried by the rewritten mapping preamble.

title: Prompter
description: Narrow Prompter interface on the Factory with TTY detection, scripted test double, and a library pick that won't rot.

title: Library pick: charmbracelet/huh for the live prompter
description:
Problem: every prompt library has trade-offs. `AlecAivazis/survey/v2`
is in maintenance mode; `charmbracelet/huh` is actively maintained
and pretty; raw `bubbletea` is too low-level to be a prompter. A
stdlib-only live prompter is doable (~120 lines + `golang.org/x/term`
for no-echo passwords) but ships an underwhelming Select/MultiSelect
UX compared to an arrow-key picker.

Idea: ship `charmbracelet/huh` as the default `prompt.NewLive` impl.
It covers Confirm / Input / Password / Select / MultiSelect with a
consistent TTY UX, degrades deterministically when stdin isn't a
terminal (coordinated with byob-prompter.3's `ErrNotTTY` sentinel), and
is actively maintained by a team that ships other CLI-adjacent
libraries.

Because the Prompter is a narrow interface (byob-prompter.1), huh's types
never leak to callers; swapping the impl later is mechanical.

Tradeoffs:

- **Transitive dep weight.** huh pulls bubbletea + lipgloss. Against
  byob-release.8's pure-Go minimalism the UX win is worth the weight,
  but it IS a meaningful ask — flag it explicitly in `go.mod`
  review.
- **Known risk: API churn.** Charmbracelet's ecosystem has shipped
  breaking changes across minor/major revisions more than once.
  The narrow interface insulates callers, but the `live` impl in
  this file will need rework on those bumps. Treat the `huh` pin
  in `go.mod` as a conscious version choice, not a floating
  dependency, and expect to spend time on updates.
- **Known risk: context cancellation is best-effort.** `huh.Run()`
  is blocking and has no native `context.Context` awareness, so
  the `live` impl runs huh in a goroutine and selects on
  `ctx.Done()`. On cancellation the prompt goroutine leaks until
  the user hits a key (or the process exits); the *caller* gets
  `ctx.Err()` immediately, which is what matters for command
  shutdown.
- **Fallback if the above risks bite.** Switch to a stdlib-only
  impl (`bufio.Scanner` + `golang.org/x/term` for no-echo
  passwords) or `AlecAivazis/survey/v2` (stable API, maintenance-
  mode but functional). Both satisfy the same `Prompter`
  interface.

title: Refuse to prompt when stdin is not a TTY
description:
Problem: a command that prompts for confirmation works interactively
but hangs in CI or in a pipeline with no stdin attached. Worse,
naive prompt libraries read EOF, interpret it as "no", and silently
skip a destructive action without failing.

Idea: every Prompter method checks `IO.IsStdinTTY()` first (byob-iostreams.1
exposes this on IOStreams). If false, return a sentinel `ErrNotTTY`.
The caller is responsible for handling it — typically by requiring
`--yes`/`-y` (see byob-prompter.5) or failing with a clear message
("pass --yes to skip confirmation in non-interactive environments").

Tradeoffs: every Prompter caller now has to think about the non-TTY
case. That's the point — the failure mode goes from "silently
wrong" to "explicitly unsupported." `--yes` (byob-prompter.5) already
covers the "skip prompts despite a TTY" case; no separate env-var
escape hatch is needed.

title: Test prompter is a scripted FIFO stub
description:
Problem: testing code that prompts the user typically involves
fragile input-simulation (writing to a pipe, racing a goroutine) or
a mocking library that hides the call sequence.

Idea: a `Stub` type that holds per-method FIFOs. Each call pops the
next value. Over-consumption panics (loud failure beats silent
incorrect answer). Ordering matches the call order in the test — if
the test expects "Confirm, then Input, then Select", the stub's
slices are sized accordingly.

Aligns with byob-testing.1 (test doubles through the Factory, no
monkey-patching) — the stub replaces `f.Prompter` directly; no
library-level patching is needed.

Tradeoffs: when a command changes the order of its prompts, the
test slice doesn't auto-resize — you update the slice, which is
exactly the right level of refactor pain. For commands that branch
the prompt order based on prior answers, the stub's per-method
FIFOs are not order-preserving across methods; write a record-calls
helper if that matters.

title: --yes / -y destructive-action override
description:
Problem: destructive actions (delete, purge, overwrite) need
confirmation when run interactively and must be bypassable in CI
scripts. Tools that invent their own flag (`--force`, `--no-confirm`,
`--non-interactive`) end up with three inconsistent flags across
subcommands.

Idea: one flag, `--yes` (short `-y`), on any command that does a
destructive action. When set, `Confirm()` returns true without
prompting. Documented convention across the tool — every destroyer
reads the same flag.

`--yes` is NOT a persistent root flag, because not every command is
destructive. It's a per-command flag, but the flag name and
semantics are template-mandated so users see a uniform surface.

Tradeoffs: users who want a single "assume yes to everything" knob
have to learn that it's per-command. That's correct — a persistent
`--yes` would silently confirm destructive side-effects in
subcommands the user didn't intend to flag.

Relationship to `ErrNotTTY` (byob-prompter.3): `--yes` short-circuits the
TTY check. A non-interactive run with `--yes` is the supported,
correct flow. A non-interactive run without `--yes` returns
`ErrNotTTY` and fails with a clear message.

title: Release
description: Pure-Go discipline (CGO_ENABLED=0, go:embed) as the foundation; Makefile+ldflags for day-to-day builds; goreleaser for tag-triggered cross-compile, archives, checksums, optional homebrew/nfpm channels. Both paths inject the same ldflags vars so version output is path-independent.

title: Version via -ldflags -X into a dedicated build package
description:
Problem: the binary needs to know its own version, commit, and build
date at runtime. Options: ldflags-injected package vars,
`debug.ReadBuildInfo()`, a hand-maintained `version.go` constant, a
generated file. Each has gaps — constants go stale, generated files
churn, BuildInfo is empty or partial under `go build` from a dirty
tree or from an archive extraction.

Idea: a small package `internal/<bin>cmd/build` exposes three
package-scope vars with sentinel defaults (named constants so
consumers test against one symbol, not a string literal):

```go
const (
    VersionDev  = "dev"
    CommitNone  = "none"
    DateUnknown = "unknown"
)
var (
    Version = VersionDev
    Commit  = CommitNone
    Date    = DateUnknown
)
```

Both the Makefile and `.goreleaser.yml` inject the same ldflags so
every build path populates the same three vars:

```
-ldflags "-X <pkg>/build.Version=$(VERSION)
         -X <pkg>/build.Commit=$(COMMIT)
         -X <pkg>/build.Date=$(DATE)"
```

`debug.ReadBuildInfo()` is a **secondary** source inside the build
package: when `Version == VersionDev` (no ldflags), an `Info()`
accessor consults BuildInfo for VCS revision + dirty flag so plain
`go install github.com/x/y@latest` still produces a usable `version`
output.

Thread-safety: `Info()` must not mutate the package vars from its
read path. Two parallel test packages calling `build.Info()`
concurrently would race. Compute the augmented values into locals
and return them; wrap in `sync.OnceValue` (single-return — the
closure never errors) so the `debug.ReadBuildInfo` scan runs at
most once per process.

Tradeoffs: ldflags strings are verbose and easy to typo — hence the
shared Makefile variable both the local `build` target and the GHA
release workflow reference. A single source of truth for the flag
string prevents drift between dev and release builds.

title: Stdlib-first; reach for deps only when the stdlib is genuinely insufficient
description:
Problem: every direct dependency is a permanent maintenance commitment
— security updates, breaking changes, transitive bloat, the risk that
an upstream goes unmaintained. The Go standard library covers most of
what a CLI needs (`net/http`, `encoding/json`, `os/exec`, `log/slog`,
`database/sql`, `context`, `flag`/`pflag`), and the gap between
"writing it myself with stdlib" and "pulling a wrapper library" is
usually a hundred lines that the wrapper would have written anyway —
but without the wrapper's API surface, version pinning, and
supply-chain risk.

Idea: the default is the standard library. Reach for an external
dependency only when the stdlib is genuinely insufficient *and* the
dep itself follows pure-Go discipline (byob-release.8). The two
decisions stack: byob-release.8 is the floor any accepted dep must
clear (pure-Go); this decision is the prior question of whether to
take a dep at all. The blessed exceptions byob ships are:

- `github.com/spf13/cobra` — the CLI command tree (byob-command-shape).
  Stdlib `flag` doesn't do subcommand trees.
- `github.com/google/go-cmp` — non-trivial test diffs
  (byob-testing.2). Stdlib `reflect.DeepEqual` returns a boolean with
  no diff.
- `modernc.org/sqlite` — pure-Go SQLite driver (byob-release.8). No
  stdlib equivalent.
- `github.com/goreleaser/goreleaser` — release matrix (build-time
  only, not a runtime dep) (byob-release.4).

Each exception has a decision bead that justifies it. A new dependency
proposal needs the same form: name the stdlib API it replaces, explain
why that API is insufficient *for this CLI*, and confirm the dep is
pure-Go.

Tradeoffs: writing it yourself takes longer than `go get` and pasting
a snippet from the README. The payoff is a smaller `go.sum`, faster
builds, fewer security-advisory false alarms, and a codebase that
survives upstream churn. For a CLI whose lifetime is measured in
years, the math favors stdlib-first by a wide margin.

When not to use: prototypes and spikes. If you're sketching to learn
whether an idea works at all, grab the dep. Before the prototype
becomes the real thing, re-evaluate every dep against the stdlib-first
test below.
design:
A worked example. The HTTP client (byob-http-client) is `net/http.Client`
with a configured `Transport` — not `resty`, not `req`, not
`gentleman`. The stdlib gives you:

```go
client := &http.Client{
    Timeout: 30 * time.Second,
    Transport: &http.Transport{
        MaxIdleConns:        100,
        IdleConnTimeout:     90 * time.Second,
        TLSHandshakeTimeout: 10 * time.Second,
    },
}

req, err := http.NewRequestWithContext(ctx, http.MethodGet, url, nil)
if err != nil {
    return fmt.Errorf("building request: %w", err)
}
req.Header.Set("User-Agent", userAgent)

resp, err := client.Do(req)
if err != nil {
    return fmt.Errorf("requesting %s %s: %w", req.Method, req.URL, err)
}
defer resp.Body.Close()
```

That's the entire HTTP layer for a typical CLI. Wrappers add: a fluent
builder, automatic retries (which you usually want explicit anyway),
automatic JSON marshalling (one line of `json.NewEncoder`), and an
API surface to learn. None of that meets the "stdlib genuinely
insufficient" bar.

Test for a proposed new dep:

1. Could the stdlib do it in a small helper file? If yes, write the
   helper.
2. Is the dep pure-Go (byob-release.8)? If no, hard stop.
3. Does the dep itself follow a similar stdlib-first discipline?
   Transitive bloat compounds.
4. Can you name the existing decision that justifies it — or do you
   need to file a new decision capturing the rationale?

If steps 1–4 all clear, add the dep and the corresponding decision
bead in the same PR. A new dep without a decision is the shape that
accretes into an unmaintainable `go.sum` over time.

title: version subcommand + --version flag on root
description:
Problem: users expect both `mytool --version` (a one-liner) and
`mytool version` (a richer block showing commit, build date, Go
version, OS/arch). Implementing them separately drifts. Implementing
only `--version` fails the user who pastes the version subcommand
into a bug report and wants the full block.

Idea: wire `--version` to cobra's built-in `Version` field (one-line
format string); ship a `version` subcommand that prints the richer
block. Both read from the same `build.Info()` accessor (byob-release.1)
so they can't disagree.

Format:

```
mytool <version>                      # --version (short)

mytool <version>                      # mytool version (long)
  commit: <sha>
  built:  <iso-date>
  go:     <go-version>
  os:     <goos>/<goarch>
```

Tradeoffs: two code paths for the same data; kept trivially
consistent by routing both to one formatter function. Worth the
minor duplication for the UX win.

title: Makefile is the day-to-day entrypoint
description:
Problem: `go build` + `go test` + `go install` works for single-file
demos. Real tools want `make build`, `make test`, `make lint`,
`make clean` plus a way to invoke the release pipeline locally
(dry-run an archive build). A shell script works; a Makefile works
better for target dependencies and partial rebuilds.

Idea: the Makefile owns every dev entrypoint. Targets:

- `build` — host binary at `./bin/mytool` with ldflags (byob-release.1)
  and reproducibility flags (byob-release.6).
- `install` — `go install` with the same flags.
- `test` — `go test -race ./...`.
- `lint` — `golangci-lint run` (when configured).
- `clean` — remove `bin/` and cached artifacts.
- `release` — shell out to `goreleaser release --clean` (byob-release.4).
- `snapshot` — `goreleaser build --snapshot --clean` for local
  dry-run of the cross-compile matrix.

Version / commit / date are computed once at the top of the Makefile
from `git describe --tags --always --dirty` and exported as
`LDFLAGS`. The Makefile injects that string into dev builds;
goreleaser (byob-release.4) computes its own `{{.Version}}` from the
release tag and injects that into release builds. The two strings
are intentionally different: `make build` on a post-tag or dirty
tree produces `v1.0.0-5-g1234567-dirty`, while goreleaser on the
same tag produces `1.0.0`. The invariant worth preserving is not
"same string" but "every binary stamps its own version via ldflags
on `internal/<bin>cmd/build`" — so `mytool version` always reports
the build's own provenance regardless of which path built it.

Tradeoffs: Makefile syntax is finicky (tab indentation, recursive
expansion, `.PHONY` discipline). The payoff is a muscle-memory
entrypoint every Go developer already uses. Alternative: a
`task`/`just`/`mage` file — each less standard than Makefile.
design:
```makefile
BIN        := mytool
VERSION    := $(shell git describe --tags --always --dirty 2>/dev/null || echo dev)
COMMIT     := $(shell git rev-parse HEAD 2>/dev/null || echo none)
DATE       := $(shell date -u +%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ)
PKG        := github.com/acme/$(BIN)/internal/$(BIN)cmd/build

# Dev LDFLAGS keep symbols so delve / pprof / stack traces work.
# byob-release.6 handles the -s -w strip in .goreleaser.yml for release.
LDFLAGS    := -X $(PKG).Version=$(VERSION) \
              -X $(PKG).Commit=$(COMMIT) \
              -X $(PKG).Date=$(DATE)
# Not named GOFLAGS — that is a reserved Go env var (the toolchain
# prepends its value to every `go` invocation). Exporting it would
# double-apply -trimpath.
GO_BUILD_FLAGS := -trimpath
export LDFLAGS VERSION COMMIT DATE

.PHONY: build install test lint clean release snapshot
build:
	CGO_ENABLED=0 go build $(GO_BUILD_FLAGS) -ldflags "$(LDFLAGS)" -o bin/$(BIN) ./cmd/$(BIN)

install:
	CGO_ENABLED=0 go install $(GO_BUILD_FLAGS) -ldflags "$(LDFLAGS)" ./cmd/$(BIN)

test:
	go test -race ./...

release:
	goreleaser release --clean

snapshot:
	goreleaser build --snapshot --clean
```

Cross-compile matrix does **not** live in the Makefile — that's
goreleaser's job (byob-release.4). The Makefile orchestrates; goreleaser
does the matrix.

title: goreleaser owns the release cross-compile matrix
description:
Problem: a hand-rolled Makefile that loops over GOOS/GOARCH and
produces `.tar.gz`/`.zip` archives with SHA256 checksums, a Homebrew
formula, and optional deb/rpm packages is 200 lines of shell that
drifts. Managing these concerns by hand is exactly where release
tooling pays rent.

Idea: `.goreleaser.yml` configures:

- `builds[]`: linux/darwin/windows × amd64/arm64 (extend as the
  audience requires).
- `archives[]`: tar.gz for unix, zip for windows, consistent naming.
- `checksum`: single `SHA256SUMS` file alongside the archives.
- `brews[]`: optional Homebrew tap (update a formula repo on
  release).
- `nfpms[]`: optional deb/rpm packages for linux distros.
- Same ldflags as the Makefile (byob-release.1) for version injection.

Invoked two ways:

- `make release` → `goreleaser release --clean` (run from the
  release GitHub Action on a `v*` tag).
- `make snapshot` → `goreleaser build --snapshot --clean` for local
  dry-run without publishing.

Tradeoffs: one more tool to learn (goreleaser's YAML schema) and one
more dep in CI (`goreleaser` must be installed in the runner).
Offset: homebrew formula management, checksum files, and archive
naming conventions are exactly the kind of bookkeeping a hand-rolled
Makefile gets wrong the third time.
design:
```yaml
# .goreleaser.yml
version: 2

builds:
  - id: mytool
    main: ./cmd/mytool
    binary: mytool
    env: [CGO_ENABLED=0]
    flags: [-trimpath]
    ldflags:
      - -s -w
      - -X github.com/acme/mytool/internal/mytoolcmd/build.Version={{.Version}}
      - -X github.com/acme/mytool/internal/mytoolcmd/build.Commit={{.FullCommit}}
      - -X github.com/acme/mytool/internal/mytoolcmd/build.Date={{.Date}}
    goos: [linux, darwin, windows]
    goarch: [amd64, arm64]

archives:
  - format: tar.gz
    format_overrides: [{ goos: windows, format: zip }]
    name_template: "{{ .ProjectName }}_{{ .Version }}_{{ .Os }}_{{ .Arch }}"

checksum:
  name_template: "SHA256SUMS"
  algorithm: sha256

brews:
  - repository: { owner: acme, name: homebrew-tap }
    directory: Formula
    homepage: https://github.com/acme/mytool
    description: A CLI tool.
    license: BSD-3-Clause
```

The Makefile and goreleaser deliberately produce different
`build.Version` strings — see byob-release.3 for the split. What they
share is the invariant that every binary's `version` output comes
from `-X` ldflags on the `internal/<bin>cmd/build` package, not
from runtime guesswork. That is the invariant worth preserving.

title: Release workflow: tag-triggered GHA invokes goreleaser
description:
Problem: running `goreleaser release` from a developer laptop works
but mints a release from unreproducible state (laptop-specific Go
toolchain, environment variables, possibly uncommitted files). A
tag-triggered GitHub Action runs from a clean checkout with a pinned
Go version.

Idea: `.github/workflows/release.yml` triggers on `v*` tag push.
Steps:

1. `actions/checkout@v4` with `fetch-depth: 0` (goreleaser needs
   full git history for `git describe`).
2. `actions/setup-go@v5` pinned to the project's current Go version.
3. `goreleaser/goreleaser-action@v6` running `release --clean`.

The workflow needs `GITHUB_TOKEN` (automatic) for release creation
and archive upload, and `HOMEBREW_TAP_TOKEN` (manual secret) if a
homebrew tap is configured.

Any project-specific release artifacts (e.g. the byob template
itself exports `.beads/issues.jsonl`) are attached as **separate**
workflow steps that upload to the same GitHub release after
goreleaser finishes — don't try to make goreleaser manage them.

Tradeoffs: the workflow is declarative and re-runnable. The runner's
Go version is pinned in the YAML, so an old release tag rebuilt
months later still uses its original toolchain. Only caveat: a tag
accidentally pushed triggers a publish. Use a release branch
convention if that's a concern.
design:
```yaml
# .github/workflows/release.yml
name: release
on:
  push:
    tags: ['v*']

permissions:
  contents: write

jobs:
  goreleaser:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
        with: { fetch-depth: 0 }
      - uses: actions/setup-go@v5
        with: { go-version: '1.24' }
      - uses: goreleaser/goreleaser-action@v6
        with:
          version: latest
          args: release --clean
        env:
          GITHUB_TOKEN: ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}

      # Byob-only: publish the decision/memory export as a release asset.
      # Projects that aren't byob-shaped can delete this step.
      - name: upload byob issues.jsonl
        run: make export && gh release upload ${{ github.ref_name }} .beads/issues.jsonl
        env:
          GH_TOKEN: ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}
```

title: Reproducibility flags: -trimpath always, -s -w on release only
description:
Problem: `-s -w` strips the binary's symbol table and DWARF debug
info. It's the right default for a release binary (smaller download,
slightly faster load) and the wrong default for a dev build — it
breaks `delve`, `pprof`, and useful stack traces. Applying it
uniformly trades debuggability for file size everywhere.

Idea: split the flag sets:

- **Dev builds** (`make build`, `make install`, `go run`):
  `-trimpath` only. Path-free binaries, full symbols.
- **Release builds** (`make release` via goreleaser):
  `-trimpath -ldflags "-s -w"`. Stripped + path-free.

`-trimpath` stays on both because it has no debugging downside — it
just removes local filesystem paths from the binary, which is good
hygiene regardless.

Pair both with `CGO_ENABLED=0` (byob-release.8) for pure-Go, static
binaries that cross-compile without a C toolchain.

Reproducibility caveat: `-trimpath` + `-s -w` + `CGO_ENABLED=0` is
**not** byte-reproducible by itself. The `Date` ldflag alone defeats
it, and reproducible Go builds also need `SOURCE_DATE_EPOCH` handling
and a pinned Go toolchain version. This decision doesn't aim for
byte-reproducibility; it aims for small, path-free release binaries
and fully debuggable dev binaries. Pursue full reproducibility only
if downstream distributors require it.
design:
```makefile
# Makefile — dev build keeps symbols. Not named GOFLAGS (that's a
# reserved Go env var).
GO_BUILD_FLAGS := -trimpath
LDFLAGS := -X $(PKG).Version=$(VERSION) \
           -X $(PKG).Commit=$(COMMIT) \
           -X $(PKG).Date=$(DATE)
build:
	CGO_ENABLED=0 go build $(GO_BUILD_FLAGS) -ldflags "$(LDFLAGS)" -o bin/$(BIN) ./cmd/$(BIN)
```

```yaml
# .goreleaser.yml — release strips symbols:
builds:
  - env: [CGO_ENABLED=0]
    flags: [-trimpath]
    ldflags:
      - -s -w
      - -X github.com/acme/mytool/internal/mytoolcmd/build.Version={{.Version}}
      # ...etc
```

Same `-trimpath`, different `-s -w`. Dev binaries are debuggable;
release binaries are lean.

title: Recommended .golangci.yml: pin the lint floor byob idioms assume
description:
Problem: byob-release.3 names `golangci-lint run` as the body of `make lint`,
but golangci-lint v2 ships with most useful linters disabled by default.
Without a pinned `.golangci.yml`, the rules byob's idioms quietly assume
(consistent initialism casing, exported-doc shape, errcheck on every
return) aren't enforced — agents drift, fresh code accumulates lint
debt, and the memory layer that names these rules is paper protection.

Idea: ship a recommended `.golangci.yml` that enables the linters byob
relies on, with a small allowlist of overrides for cases the template's
idioms generate (e.g. `noctx` off in `_test.go` because test helpers
legitimately use background context).

Enable, at minimum:
- `errcheck` — every returned error is handled or annotated.
- `staticcheck` — SA bug-checks plus the ST naming rules, especially
  ST1003 (initialism casing).
- `revive` with `exported`, `var-naming`, `receiver-naming`,
  `unused-receiver` — covers the doc-comment-shape and the Get-prefix /
  initialism naming memories.
- `gocritic` — opinionated correctness/style.
- `govet` with `nilness` and `shadow` — backstop for the typed-nil
  return-signature decision (byob-errors.5).
- `ineffassign`, `unused` — dead-code hygiene.

Plus `goimports` (formatter) for import group order matching byob's
stdlib / third-party / project convention.

Tradeoffs: more friction on legacy code being ported into a byob-shaped
layout. byob targets greenfield Go CLI tools, so the cost is small at
template-instantiation time and only grows if you defer adoption. The
config is opt-in (the file ships in the template; targets edit it).

When not to use: never. If you remove the lint floor you also remove
the `golangci-lint` invocation from `make lint`; otherwise the makefile
target lies about what it's checking.
design:
```yaml
# .golangci.yml — pinned defaults for byob-shaped Go CLIs.
# Schema is golangci-lint v2.

version: "2"

linters:
  default: none
  enable:
    - errcheck
    - staticcheck
    - revive
    - gocritic
    - govet
    - ineffassign
    - unused

  settings:
    staticcheck:
      checks:
        - all
        - "-ST1000"  # package comment — not mandated on internal pkgs
    revive:
      rules:
        - name: exported
        - name: var-naming
        - name: receiver-naming
        - name: unused-receiver
    govet:
      enable:
        - nilness
        - shadow

  exclusions:
    rules:
      # Test helpers legitimately use context.Background() and unkeyed
      # struct literals for fakes — silence those classes in _test.go.
      - path: _test\.go
        linters:
          - noctx
          - govet

formatters:
  enable:
    - goimports
  settings:
    goimports:
      local-prefixes:
        - github.com/<your-org>/<bin>
```

Replace `<your-org>/<bin>` at template-instantiation time so the
project-local import group lands in the third position
(stdlib / third-party / project).

title: Pure-Go discipline (CGO_ENABLED=0, go:embed) as the release foundation
description:
Problem: CGO makes cross-compilation a toolchain puzzle. Non-embedded assets
mean shipping a tarball instead of a binary. Users hit "install
libsqlite3-dev" on day one.

Idea: build with `CGO_ENABLED=0`. Use pure-Go implementations for anything
that traditionally required C — `modernc.org/sqlite` for SQLite, pure-Go
crypto, pure-Go tls. Ship every asset (SQL migrations, templates, static
files) via `go:embed`.

Payoff: one binary, trivial cross-compile (`GOOS=darwin GOARCH=arm64 go
build`), no install docs beyond "download and run", no runtime filesystem
layout to document.

Tradeoffs: some pure-Go drivers are slower than their C counterparts. For
typical CLI workloads — opening a sqlite file, running a few hundred
queries — the gap is invisible. Benchmark if you have a hot loop.
design:
In `go.mod`, prefer pure-Go drivers:

```
require (
    modernc.org/sqlite v1.x.x
    github.com/spf13/cobra v1.x.x
)
```

Embed assets directly into the binary:

```go
//go:embed migrations/*.sql
var migrationsFS embed.FS

//go:embed templates/*.tmpl
var templatesFS embed.FS
```

Build with CGO off, cross-compile by setting `GOOS`/`GOARCH`:

```sh
CGO_ENABLED=0 go build -trimpath -ldflags="-s -w" ./cmd/mytool
GOOS=darwin  GOARCH=arm64 CGO_ENABLED=0 go build ...
GOOS=windows GOARCH=amd64 CGO_ENABLED=0 go build ...
```

title: Lint config lands first; fix lint findings as they appear
description:
Problem: a `.golangci.yml` added after the codebase has grown surfaces
hundreds of pre-existing findings on the first run. The realistic
responses are all bad: silence the rule globally (the lint floor
degrades), `//nolint` past every finding (the noise hides real bugs),
or schedule a multi-day cleanup PR (it never lands). The lint config
from byob-release.7 only does its job if it lands when the codebase is
small enough that the first run produces zero findings.

Idea: in any new project, `.golangci.yml` (byob-release.7) and the
`make lint` target (byob-release.3) land in the first commit alongside
the cobra scaffold. In a brown-field adoption, they land in the first
commit after `bd import` of the byob beads — before the first task bead
is implemented. CI runs `make lint` alongside `make test` on every
push, and the build breaks on findings the same way it breaks on test
failures.

The cadence after that:

- Run `make lint` before every commit, alongside `make test` — the
  same pre-commit gate byob-testing.4 step 5 names, with both checks
  enforced.
- Treat new findings as build breakage. Either fix the code or fix
  the lint config — never `//nolint` past one without a comment naming
  the specific reason it's the right call for that line.
- When adding a new linter or tightening an existing rule, do it in
  its own commit and fix the resulting findings in the same commit.
  Linter changes that defer cleanup re-create the original problem at
  a smaller scale.

Tradeoffs: upfront friction during scaffolding — the first `make lint`
after wiring it up may surface findings the agent has to fix before the
initial commit lands. That's the design: the cost is small when the
codebase is empty and grows linearly with deferral. Late adoption is
exactly what the decision exists to prevent.

When not to use: if you've decided lint isn't worth the cost for this
project, remove the `golangci-lint` invocation from `make lint`
(byob-release.3) rather than letting the target lie about what it's
checking. The shape this decision exists to prevent is the half-measure
where the lint config exists but its findings are routinely ignored —
an opt-out is honest, a lying target is not.
design:
Wire `make lint` into CI alongside `make test`:

```yaml
# .github/workflows/ci.yml — relevant steps.
- name: Test
  run: make test
- name: Lint
  run: make lint
```

For a brown-field adoption with an existing codebase, the only honest
sequencing is:

1. Land `.golangci.yml` and `make lint`.
2. In the *same* commit (or the immediately following one), fix or
   carefully `//nolint` every finding from the first run. Each
   `//nolint` carries a comment naming why the finding is the wrong
   call for that line. None of: "TODO clean this up later."
3. Land CI enforcement.

If step 2 produces a diff that's too large to land at once, the lint
floor is the wrong shape for the codebase as it stands — narrow it
(drop a linter, add an exclusion in `.golangci.yml`) until step 2 fits
in one PR. A change that splits into "land the config, land the
cleanup" with weeks in between is exactly the deferred-cleanup failure
mode this decision exists to prevent.

title: Runtime directories
description: Per-OS directories for cache, state, and data (config is covered in byob-config), plus the atomic-write discipline that keeps them consistent under concurrent invocations.

title: Four-directory model: config / cache / state / data
description:
Problem: CLIs that dump everything into `~/.mytool/` conflate
user-editable config with regenerable cache, persistent state, and
shipped data. Cleaning a user's cache then destroys their config.
Following XDG on Linux but not macOS/Windows means platform users
get inconsistent experiences.

Idea: three distinct directories, each resolved per-OS via the
stdlib where possible and an in-repo helper for state (the stdlib
has no `UserStateDir`):

- **config** — `os.UserConfigDir()` (covered by byob-config for the
  walk-up discovery). User-editable, small, rarely changes.
  Linux: `~/.config/mytool/`; macOS: `~/Library/Application Support/mytool/`;
  Windows: `%AppData%\mytool\`.
- **cache** — `os.UserCacheDir()` joined with tool name. Regenerable,
  safe to `rm -rf`. Fetched data, compiled templates, thumbnail
  blobs, anything the tool can recreate on demand. Windows:
  `%LocalAppData%\mytool\`.
- **state** — an in-repo `paths.stateDir()` helper joined with tool
  name. Non-user-editable but persistent: last-used-repo, undo
  history, auth state (when added later), run counters. Lost-state
  is annoying but not destructive.
  - Unix: `$XDG_STATE_HOME` → `$HOME/.local/state`.
  - macOS: `$HOME/Library/Application Support/<tool>` (shared with
    config; distinguish by subfolder).
  - Windows: `%LocalAppData%\<tool>` (same directory as cache;
    distinguish by subfolder).

Application-shipped templates or plugins ("data") aren't a separate
category here — when a tool needs them, pick cache or state per
regenerability and nest under the chosen root.

Each directory is `MkdirAll`'d on first use, not at startup — a
plain `mytool --version` touches zero directories.

Tradeoffs: three path concepts instead of one. Worth it: a
well-shaped tool can answer "where does X live?" from category
alone, and users can `rm -rf $(mytool paths cache)` confident they
haven't lost config. The stdlib lacks a `UserStateDir`, so the
state resolver is 30 lines of `runtime.GOOS` branching — the one
wart of this scheme.

title: Paths on the Factory as a lazy field
description:
Problem: every command that touches state or cache needs the
resolved paths. Computing them in each command re-runs
`os.UserConfigDir()` etc. redundantly and loses a single test
injection point. A package-level global makes tests non-parallel-safe.

Idea: put `Paths()` on the Factory as a lazy `sync.OnceValue`
closure, mirroring byob-config.3 (config), byob-factory-di.1 (Factory shape),
and the `sync-oncevalue` memory. First caller pays the resolution
cost; subsequent callers get the cached value. Tests override
`f.Paths` with a struct pointing at `t.TempDir()` subdirectories,
keeping each test hermetic (per the `test-tempdir` memory).

Tradeoffs: one more lazy field on the Factory. The laziness is
load-bearing: it means `mytool --version` and `mytool --help` pay no
filesystem cost at all (aligned with byob-config.3's cold-start
argument).

title: Atomic writes: temp-in-same-dir + fsync + rename; flock for read-modify-write
description:
Problem: two failure modes bite concurrent CLI invocations:

1. **Torn writes.** `os.WriteFile(path, data, perm)` can crash
   mid-write and leave a truncated file. A reader in another
   invocation sees half a JSON document.
2. **Lost updates.** Two processes doing read-modify-write on the
   same state file can each read the old version, each write their
   update, and silently clobber each other — both "atomic renames,"
   one lost edit.

Idea: two disciplines, applied where each matters.

- **Atomic write (all state files):** create a temp file in the
  **same directory** as the target (cross-dir renames aren't atomic
  on POSIX), write the full payload, `f.Sync()`, then
  `os.Rename(tmp, final)`. Also `fsync` the parent directory after
  rename for durability on kernel crash. Wrap in a `WriteFileAtomic`
  helper so every call site gets it right.
- **File lock (read-modify-write):** advisory lock via `flock(2)`
  (use `golang.org/x/sys/unix.Flock` on POSIX;
  `syscall.LockFileEx` on Windows) held for the duration of the
  read-compute-write cycle. Lock file is a sibling of the state file
  (`state.json.lock`). Alternative: a CAS-via-version field in the
  state itself (retry on conflict) — useful when you can't take a
  lock (e.g. state on a network filesystem).

Tradeoffs: flock is advisory — well-behaved processes respect it;
rogue ones ignore it. That's fine for a single CLI talking to its
own state. For true multi-writer scenarios, sqlite (byob-storage) gives
you real transactions. JSON state + flock is the "small, structured
state" answer; sqlite is the "more than ~1KB of structured state"
answer.

title: State schema versioning: refuse newer, upgrade older
description:
Problem: a tool at v2 reading a state file written by v3 (a user
downgraded, or ran two versions on the same machine) can silently
drop fields it doesn't understand. A tool at v2 reading a v1 file
can fail to parse because a required field is missing. Both failure
modes are silent by default; both corrupt the user's state.

Idea: every persistent state file (JSON, TOML, whatever) carries a
top-level `schema_version` integer field. Writers stamp the current
version. Readers:

- **`stored > current`**: refuse to parse. Print an error naming
  the stored version, the current version, and suggest updating the
  tool. Do NOT touch the file.
- **`stored < current`**: upgrade-on-read. A per-version migration
  function transforms the file from `v1 → v2 → v3 → current`.
  Writer-side write-back happens on the next normal save; readers
  don't need to mutate on disk.
- **`stored == current`**: parse normally.

SQLite state (byob-storage) handles schema versioning via its own
migrations; this decision is specifically for JSON/TOML files that
sit outside a DB.

Tradeoffs: every schema change requires a migration function. That's
the discipline that prevents silent data loss. For state that's
purely a cache (regenerable), skip the versioning — just ignore
unreadable files and regenerate. Versioning is for state you can't
recompute.

title: Security
description: Supply-chain and secret-handling posture: pin by hash not tag, scan for known CVEs on every push, ship SBOMs and signatures from the release pipeline, and refuse to accept secrets as flag values.

title: Pin Go dependencies by exact version; never `@latest` in CI
description:
Problem: `go get example.com/pkg@latest`, `go install tool@main`, or a
Dockerfile that installs a tool without a version all produce
non-reproducible builds. Worse, if an attacker compromises a
package's `main` branch or publishes a new tag, the next CI run picks
