return concrete types (`*Factory`, `*sqlite.Store`, `*http.Client`).
Callers that only want the interface view can assign the return value to
an interface variable themselves.

Complements the "define interfaces in the consumer package" bead: together,
they say "the consumer declares a narrow interface, and the producer gives
it a concrete value that happens to satisfy that interface."

Exception: return an interface when the concrete type is a true
implementation detail that should not leak (e.g., `crc32.NewIEEE()` returns
`hash.Hash32` because the underlying type has no useful public surface).

Tradeoffs: returning concrete types means callers can depend on every
exported method of that type — which is the goal for structs you own, and
the downside for types you'd rather keep flexible. When that downside
matters, return an interface on purpose; don't do it by reflex.

When not to use: rare; this is the default posture. Deviate only when a
concrete return type would encourage coupling to internals the caller
should not care about.

title: Accept fs.FS at package boundaries for filesystem seams
description:
Problem: a package that reads files via `os.Open` or `os.ReadFile` has
baked disk I/O into its API. Tests have to create temp directories,
write fixture files, and clean up — or reach for path-rewriting hacks.
Embedded assets end up on a parallel code path.

Idea: accept `fs.FS` at package boundaries instead of string paths.
`fs.FS` is a tiny stdlib interface (`Open(name string) (fs.File,
error)`), and `fs.ReadFile`, `fs.WalkDir`, `fs.Glob`, and `fs.Sub` all
take one. In production, pass `os.DirFS("/path")`. In tests, pass
`fstest.MapFS{}` — an in-memory fake with no disk touched, no temp
dirs, no cleanup. For embedded assets, `embed.FS` already satisfies
`fs.FS`, so the same code path works for on-disk files, embedded
resources, and hermetic tests.

Tradeoffs: the interface is read-only. If your package also writes
files, keep the write path separate (accept a writer or a directory
path for writes). That's a clean split, not a leak — read and write
really are different concerns.

When not to use: for purely invocation-level file reads at a runFunc
boundary (e.g., `cmd foo --config /path/to/file`), parsing the path
and handing the parsed value down is fine. The seam is for packages
that do non-trivial filesystem work internally.

title: IOStreams
description: Single abstraction for stdin/stdout/stderr with TTY detection and color support.

title: IOStreams wraps In/Out/ErrOut + TTY flags; commands never touch os.Std*
description:
Problem: `fmt.Println`, `os.Stdout.Write`, and friends scattered across a
codebase are impossible to capture in tests and impossible to redirect
consistently (e.g., to suppress output in a JSON mode).

Idea: define a small `IOStreams` struct with `In io.Reader`, `Out io.Writer`,
`ErrOut io.Writer`, plus TTY flags for all three streams. Every command
writes through its `*IOStreams`. The only place in the codebase that
touches `os.Stdin` / `os.Stdout` / `os.Stderr` is `iostreams.System()`,
called once in `main()`.

All three streams carry their own TTY flag. Stdin's flag isn't just
symmetry: the Prompter (byob-prompter) consults `IsStdinTTY()` to decide
whether to prompt at all, so this decision has to expose it alongside
the output-stream flags.

Tradeoffs: you pay a tiny indirection. You also gain the ability to swap
buffers in tests, suppress chatter in JSON mode, and ask `IsStdoutTTY()`
without sprinkling `isatty` checks across the codebase.

title: ColorScheme honors NO_COLOR + TTY, degrades to identity function
description:
Problem: terminal color codes embedded across the codebase create three
failure modes: (1) garbage in pipes and log files, (2) ignoring the user's
`NO_COLOR` preference, (3) ugly `if isTTY` guards at every print site.

Idea: attach a `ColorScheme` to `IOStreams`. It exposes `Red(s)`, `Green(s)`,
`Bold(s)`, etc. When colors are disabled (non-TTY stdout, `NO_COLOR` env var
set, or explicit `--no-color`), those methods return the input unchanged.
Call sites always write `cs.Red("error")` without guarding.

Tradeoffs: method-per-color grows the surface slightly. Respecting the
`NO_COLOR` standard is table stakes in 2025; costs nothing to honor.

title: Data to Out, chatter and prompts to ErrOut
description:
Problem: `mytool list | wc -l` breaks when `mytool list` interleaves "Loading
items…" chatter into stdout. Users then reach for `--quiet` flags, which
multiply.

Idea: reserve `Out` for the command's DATA — the thing a user might pipe into
jq, awk, grep. Chatter (status messages, progress, prompts, warnings) goes to
`ErrOut`. Scripting users get clean stdout by default; humans still see the
progress because ErrOut isn't redirected by `|`.

Rule of thumb: if removing the print would change the meaning of piped
output, it goes to `Out`. Otherwise `ErrOut`. Prompts ALWAYS go to ErrOut
because prompts read from stdin, and stdin is usually the pipe.

Tradeoffs: authors must think about which stream a message belongs on. That
thinking is exactly the value.

title: Layout
description: Conventional directory split and cobra command grouping.

title: Three-tier layout: cmd/<bin> -> internal/<bin>cmd -> pkg/cmd/<feature>
description:
Problem: fat `main.go` files accrue flag parsing, business logic, and error
handling. Single-package `cmd/` trees force circular-import gymnastics when
commands want to share helpers.

Idea: a conventional three-tier layout.
- `cmd/<bin>/main.go` — ~20 lines. Build factory, call runner, exit with
  mapped error code.
- `internal/<bin>cmd/cmd.go` — the runner with error-type → exit-code
  mapping and any process-global concerns (signal handling, profile flag).
- `pkg/cmd/root/root.go` — root cobra command, groups, aggregates features.
- `pkg/cmd/<feature>/<feature>.go` — one NewCmdXxx per feature, each with
  its own `_test.go`.

Adding a new feature is a self-contained PR: new package under `pkg/cmd/`,
one import line in `root.go`.

Tradeoffs: more directories than a flat layout. The flat layout dies around
5 commands; this scales to 50.
design:
```
cmd/mytool/main.go               // 20 lines
internal/mytoolcmd/cmd.go        // Run(ios) int — error→exit-code mapping
pkg/cmd/root/root.go             // root cobra.Command + groups
pkg/cmdutil/factory.go           // Factory definition
pkg/cmdutil/errors.go            // FlagError, ErrHint, FlagErrorf
pkg/iostreams/iostreams.go       // IOStreams, Test(), ColorScheme
pkg/cmd/create/create.go         // NewCmdCreate(f, runF)
pkg/cmd/create/create_test.go
pkg/cmd/list/list.go
pkg/cmd/list/list_test.go
```

title: Lifecycle
description: Process-lifecycle and cancellation: signal handling, context propagation through runFuncs.

title: Thread context.Context through every runFunc
description:
Problem: a runFunc signature of `func(opts *Options) error` can't be
cancelled. Every HTTP call, DB query, or subprocess inside it is
uninterruptible, and Ctrl-C produces an orphaned child process or a stuck
database connection.

Idea: follow the Go stdlib convention: every function that might block
takes a `context.Context` as its first argument, and returns quickly when
`ctx.Done()` fires. runFuncs are no exception — make them
`func(ctx context.Context, opts *Options) error`.

`main()` constructs the root ctx (see byob-lifecycle.2 for the
`signal.NotifyContext` setup) and threads it through
`root.ExecuteContext(ctx)`. Cobra's `cmd.Context()` returns that same
context inside every RunE, so the plumbing is: pull `ctx` out of
`cmd.Context()` and pass it to your runFunc.

Tradeoffs: every blocking call inside a command now has to accept ctx and
pass it through. That's a one-time audit of your codebase, not ongoing
friction. The alternative — ignoring cancellation — produces the
user-hostile behavior described in the Problem.

When not to use: never. Context threading is table stakes in modern Go.

title: Wire Ctrl-C / SIGTERM via signal.NotifyContext in main
description:
Problem: users hit Ctrl-C and expect the CLI to stop. Naive
implementations either ignore the signal (process gets killed
uncleanly, orphaning subprocesses and DB connections) or reach for
channels, goroutines, and shutdown flags — all of which have to be
plumbed into every blocking call.

Idea: use `signal.NotifyContext(ctx, os.Interrupt, syscall.SIGTERM)`
at the top of `main()`. It returns a `context.Context` that cancels
when either signal fires. Thread that context into
`root.ExecuteContext(ctx)`, and every downstream HTTP call, DB query,
or subprocess that accepts a `context.Context` cancels automatically
— no channels, no goroutines, no shutdown flags.

Defer `cancel()` immediately after to release the signal handler on
clean exit. A second Ctrl-C then reverts to the default handler and
force-exits, which is the right behavior: the first one asks politely;
the second kills.

Tradeoffs: the catch is that your runFuncs and everything they call
must actually thread `ctx` through (see byob-lifecycle.1). If they don't,
the context cancels but nobody listens. That's a one-time audit.

When not to use: never for a production CLI. Every CLI should exit
cleanly on Ctrl-C.

title: `errgroup` as the goroutine-fanout default
description:
Problem: a CLI command that fans out N parallel calls (concurrent HTTP
fetches, parallel store reads, multiple subprocess invocations) needs
ctx cancellation, first-error short-circuit, and bounded concurrency.
Hand-rolling that with `sync.WaitGroup` + an error channel +
`context.WithCancel` invariably gets the cancellation ordering wrong on
first attempt and re-derives the same primitive across every command.

Idea: byob default for "fan out N tasks, wait, surface the first error"
is `golang.org/x/sync/errgroup` with a context-aware Group. Pick up the
ctx threaded by byob-lifecycle.1, derive a Group with
`errgroup.WithContext(ctx)`, spawn with `g.Go(func() error { ... })`,
collect with `g.Wait()`. The first non-nil error cancels the derived
ctx; every other goroutine sees `ctx.Done()` and returns. Bounded
concurrency via `g.SetLimit(n)`.

Pairs with the `goroutine-exit-path` memory: errgroup is the byob
implementation of "every goroutine has a documented exit path" for the
fanout case.

Tradeoffs: stdlib `sync.WaitGroup` + error channel works for one-off
cases and avoids a (small, well-maintained) third-party dep on
`golang.org/x/sync`. The dep is `golang.org/x` adjacent-stdlib, used
by Kubernetes, gh CLI, and most production Go — not a foreign dep. The
packaging cost is one go.mod line; the wiring cost saved is several
lines per fanout site, plus the cancellation-ordering bugs you don't
write.

When not to use:
- Long-lived background goroutines (process-lifetime workers): use
  plain ctx + select + a parent shutdown channel.
- A single goroutine spawned for parallelism inside one blocking call:
  a plain `go` + result channel is fine.
- "Fire N tasks, wait for all, collect every error" — errgroup
  short-circuits on first error. Use a `[]error` slice plus
  `errors.Join` if you need all of them.

title: Logging
description: Structured, contextual, leveled logging threaded through every command without ceremony.

title: slog as the logger, stdlib only
description:
Problem: picking a logging library (`logrus`, `zap`, `zerolog`) locks
the whole tool into that library's API, handler model, performance
envelope, and dependency footprint. Migrating later means touching
every log call site. And third-party loggers drift in and out of
maintenance while stdlib does not.

Idea: use `log/slog` from the standard library (Go 1.21+). It ships
with `TextHandler` and `JSONHandler`, has a pluggable `Handler`
interface for custom backends (redaction, routing, testing), supports
`LogAttrs` for a zero-alloc hot path, and composes with
`context.Context` via `slog.InfoContext`. No extra dependency, no
migration risk, and the API is small enough to learn in an afternoon.

Tradeoffs: slog's ecosystem of pre-built handlers (OTLP, Sentry,
file rotation) is thinner than logrus's. You'll write the occasional
custom handler — but the `Handler` interface is four methods, so
that's a weekend project, not a rewrite.

title: Logger on the Factory, injected into context
description:
Problem: two extremes both hurt. Threading `*slog.Logger` as a
parameter through every helper pollutes every signature. Using
`slog.Default()` everywhere makes per-command attributes (command
name, run ID, host) impossible without stepping on other callers'
defaults.

Idea: the Factory holds the root logger as an eager field
(`f.Logger *slog.Logger`) — the logger itself is cheap to construct
(one slog handler over `IO.ErrOut`) so it doesn't need the
`func() (T, error)` lazy-closure shape that byob-factory-di.1 reserves for
expensive deps. The root command's
`PersistentPreRunE` (byob-command-shape.5) attaches per-run attributes with
`logger.With(...)` and stuffs the result into `cmd.Context()` — the
same context already threaded through every runFunc (byob-lifecycle.1).
Command code reaches for the logger via `slog.InfoContext(ctx, ...)`
or a tiny `logs.From(ctx)` helper.

Tradeoffs: `slog.FromContext` is not stdlib — you write a 5-line
context-key helper. Not every log call site has a ctx, so a default
logger still exists as a fallback. The win: commands never pass a
logger parameter, and per-command attributes attach in one place.

title: Verbosity ladder: -v / -vv / --log-level on root
description:
Problem: users want a quick "more output" knob (`-v`), a "full debug"
knob (`-vv`), AND explicit control for scripts (`--log-level=info`).
Picking just one frustrates the others. Env-var control
(`MYTOOL_LOG=debug`) is expected by anyone who's used `gh` or
`kubectl`.

Idea: three persistent flags on root (byob-command-shape.5 pattern) with a
documented precedence:

1. `--log-level=warn|info|debug` — explicit, wins when set.
2. `-v`/`-vv` — count flag: `-v` → Info, `-vv`+ → Debug. Loses to
   `--log-level` when both are passed.
3. `MYTOOL_LOG=<level>` env var — loses to both flags, beats the
   default.
4. Default — `Warn`. The binary is quiet unless asked otherwise.

The "flags beat env" direction is deliberately opposite to byob-config.2
(which says env > file > default for *config*). Logging verbosity is
per-invocation, not per-shell; a `-vv` on the command line should not
be silenced by a stale `MYTOOL_LOG=warn` in the environment.

Tradeoffs: three knobs is one more than the lean option. Users who
only want `-v`/`-vv` can ignore the other two. Scripting users want
the explicit `--log-level` because `-vv` reads like a typo in a CI
log.

title: Logs and chatter share ErrOut; quiet default keeps them separate
description:
Problem: byob-iostreams.3 allocated `ErrOut` to human chatter (progress,
prompts, warnings). A slog handler wired to the same stream can
interleave structured log records into "Loading items…" chatter —
now `2>tool.log` captures garbage and a scripter piping stderr to
`jq` sees prose mixed with JSON.

Idea: the default log level is `Warn` (byob-logging.3), so in the common
case logs emit nothing and chatter owns ErrOut by itself. When the
user passes `-v`/`-vv`/`--log-level`, they've explicitly opted into a
mixed stream — they know what they asked for. For scripted capture
of structured output, `--log-format=json` swaps `TextHandler` to
`JSONHandler`. For full separation, `--log-file=<path>` writes logs
to a file, leaving ErrOut to chatter alone.

Rule of thumb: if the user hasn't asked for logs, don't print any.
Chatter (byob-iostreams.3) is still the primary human channel. Logs are
machine-parseable opt-in.

No `--quiet`/`-q` flag. The template deliberately omits one because
the byob-iostreams.3 / byob-logging.4 combination already gives users three
orthogonal knobs: `2>/dev/null` silences ErrOut entirely,
`--log-file=/dev/null` discards logs while keeping chatter, and the
default (no flags) is already quiet for logs. Adding `--quiet` would
overlap confusingly with these. Projects that really want one can
add a persistent `-q` that redirects `IO.ErrOut` to `io.Discard`
in `PersistentPreRunE` — that's the one-line answer.

Tradeoffs: "quiet by default" means new developers don't see logs
until they know about `-v`. That's fine — the chatter channel still
gives them what they need, and `-v` is the standard debugging
reflex for Unix tools.

The `--log-file` file handle deliberately lives for the process
lifetime; every `slog` call would need a reference otherwise. A
short-lived CLI exits and the OS reclaims it. If a tool later grows a
long-running / daemon mode, wire the close into the root command's
shutdown hook rather than deferring it next to the open.

title: Output
description: TTY-adaptive human output plus first-class structured export.

title: TTY-adaptive table printer: one API, two render paths
description:
Problem: a `list` command that prints a pretty ANSI table breaks every
pipeline. A `list` command that prints tab-separated values is unreadable in
a terminal. Users want both, and `--output=plain` is a clumsy workaround.

Idea: one table printer, two render paths. On `Render()`, branch on
`IsStdoutTTY()`. TTY path: colored headers, auto-width columns, fuzzy
timestamps ("2h ago"). Non-TTY path: tab-separated columns, RFC3339
timestamps, no color. Users never pass a flag; the tool does the right thing
based on where stdout points.

Tradeoffs: authors must remember timestamps, widths, and colors diverge
between paths. Push the divergence into the printer; commands stay simple.

title: Opt-in structured export via --json / --jq / --template
description:
Problem: scripters shouldn't have to parse your TTY output with regex. Every
serious CLI needs a structured mode.

Idea: commands that print "resources" accept three opt-in flags:
`--json <fields>` (emit JSON array with the listed fields), `--jq <expr>`
(run the JSON through a jq filter before printing), `--template <tmpl>` (run
the JSON through Go text/template). Resource types implement an
`ExportData(fields) map[string]any` method that produces a stable JSON shape
independent of the TTY rendering.

Tradeoffs: maintaining the JSON schema is a contract. Version it if needed.
Alternative: `--output=json` that emits a fixed shape — simpler but less
flexible. `--json <fields>` makes the client pick what they want.

title: Generate reference docs (Markdown, man pages) from the cobra tree
description:
Problem: hand-written man pages and Markdown docs drift out of sync the
moment you add a flag or rename a subcommand. Users read stale examples
and file bugs. Maintaining a docs site that mirrors your CLI is a
second job.

Idea: the `github.com/spf13/cobra/doc` package walks your cobra tree and
emits documentation in several formats: Markdown (`GenMarkdownTree`), man
pages (`GenManTree`), reStructuredText (`GenRestTree`), and YAML
(`GenYamlTree`). Point it at your root command and it produces one
document per subcommand, with Usage, Flags, Inherited Flags, Examples,
and See-Also cross-links. Hook it up as a `go generate` target or a
CI step so the docs site is rebuilt on every change.

Your help text becomes the authoritative source: the `Short`, `Long`, and
`Example` fields you fill in on each command are the doc body. Writing
them well is now doubly rewarded — better `--help` output *and* better
published docs.

Tradeoffs: you lose free-form prose structure in the docs — everything is
generated from command help. For most tools that's a feature, not a bug.
If you need a narrative tutorial alongside the reference, write that as a
separate hand-maintained page and keep the generated reference
authoritative.

When not to use: single-command tools where `--help` is already enough.
Also skip if you've deliberately chosen a docs style (storybook, walkthrough)
that doesn't map to one-page-per-command.

title: Progress
description: Adaptive progress that looks right on a TTY and degrades off-TTY. Spinners for unknown-total, bars for known-total.

title: Progress as a narrow interface on the Factory
description:
Problem: every spinner/bar library (`charmbracelet/bubbles`,
`schollz/progressbar`, `briandowns/spinner`) exposes a different
shape. Baking one into command code couples every caller to that
library and makes the test path awkward.

Idea: a narrow interface constructed per-operation via the Factory
(byob-interfaces.1). Not a field — a factory method, because each progress
instance is operation-scoped. The interface has four methods:
`Start()`, `Update(msg string)`, `Stop()`, `Fail(err error)`.
`Stop` and `Fail(err)` are mutually-exclusive terminal states —
exactly one is called per operation, after any number of `Update`s.
Calling either after the operation has already terminated is a no-op.
Consumer code is library-agnostic; the interface lives in
`pkg/cmd/progress/`.

Factory shape: `f.Progress(ctx context.Context, label string)
progress.Progress`. The returned instance encapsulates the
TTY-vs-logging decision (byob-progress.2) internally so callers don't
branch on it. The `ctx` is captured at construction and watched
inside the impl: if it cancels mid-operation the impl calls its
own `Stop()` so the spinner doesn't keep rendering under a dead
command. Happy-path `Stop`/`Fail` still belongs to the caller
(usually `defer p.Stop()` right after `p.Start()`).

Tradeoffs: four methods is deliberately thin. No nested sub-progress,
no multi-line bars, no simultaneous concurrent progresses. Tools
that need those add them as separate interfaces (`ProgressGroup`),
not by stretching this one.

title: TTY-adaptive: spinner on TTY, rate-limited chatter lines off-TTY
description:
Problem: a spinner on a non-TTY (CI logs, piped stderr) emits ANSI
control characters and `\r` carriage returns that turn the log into
garbage. Suppressing progress entirely off-TTY loses useful signal
for long operations.

Idea: mirror byob-output.1 (TTY-adaptive table printer). The progress
interface has two concrete impls behind it:

- **TTY path:** animated spinner with `\r`-refresh, written to
  `IO.ErrOut`. Colored if `IO.ColorScheme()` allows (byob-iostreams.2).
- **Off-TTY path:** periodic plain-text lines to `IO.ErrOut`,
  rate-limited to one line every ~2 seconds, no ANSI. Uses the same
  chatter channel byob-iostreams.3 already allocated to ErrOut.

Critically, the off-TTY path writes **chatter**, not slog records.
Writing structured logs from progress contradicts byob-logging.4 (logs
default-off). Progress should show something in CI at default log
level, so it uses `fmt.Fprintln(io.ErrOut, ...)` directly.

Tradeoffs: the chatter-line path is one-way — no overwrite, each
line adds to the log. That's fine in CI where logs scroll, and
avoids the ANSI mess. TTY users still get the animated UX.

title: Library pick: bubbles/spinner + schollz/progressbar, wrapped
description:
Problem: rendering a spinner or a progress bar portably across
Windows, macOS, and Linux terminals is more code than it looks — ANSI
cursor movement, terminal-width detection, `\r`-handling when the
terminal scrolls, SIGWINCH response. Writing it in-house is possible
but fiddly and off the tool's main value path.

Idea: wrap two libraries behind the Progress interface (byob-progress.1):

- **`charmbracelet/bubbles/spinner`** for unknown-total operations.
  It's a bubbletea component, so the impl runs a tiny `tea.Program`
  and drives it via messages. The transitive weight (bubbletea +
  lipgloss) is already paid by byob-prompter.2's huh pick, so the
  marginal cost here is a direct import line, not a new dep tree.
  In exchange: a maintained, themeable spinner aligned with the
  same rendering stack the prompter uses.
- **`schollz/progressbar/v3`** for known-total operations. Pure-Go,
  actively maintained, drop-in for the fetch-and-iterate case —
  kept standalone to avoid forcing every caller to reason about a
  bubbletea `Program` for trivial progress.

Neither type escapes the `progress` package; callers see the
`Progress` interface only. This preserves the option to replace the
impl later (e.g. consolidate both paths on `bubbles/progress` when
the tool grows a richer TUI).

When to graduate further: when the tool acquires a non-trivial TUI
(dashboard, multi-pane, form-driven flows), consolidate the
known-total path on `bubbles/progress` too and drop schollz. Until
then, keeping a dedicated progress-bar impl avoids bubbletea
ceremony on the hot fetch path.

Tradeoffs:

- **Bubbletea ceremony for the spinner.** bubbles/spinner is not a
  `.Start()`/`.Stop()` wrapper — the impl has an `Init`/`Update`/
  `View` model and a goroutine running `tea.Program.Run()`.
  Heavier than a procedural spinner, but worth it for the
  maintenance story and the alignment with byob-prompter.2's rendering
  stack.
- **Prior pick (`briandowns/spinner`) was tiny but dormant.** This
  decision previously wrapped it on a "small, stable API"
  argument; upstream activity has dropped and the low-cost
  argument stopped outweighing the bitrot risk. The swap to
  bubbles accepts more ceremony in exchange for an active
  maintainer.
- **Pure-Go budget intact.** Both bubbletea and schollz honor
  byob-release.8 (no CGO).

title: Progress writes to ErrOut, never Out
description:
Problem: a spinner or bar written to stdout destroys pipeability.
`mytool fetch | jq .` gets `\r`-animated ANSI codes in its input
stream, and the `jq` parse fails — or worse, silently succeeds on
garbage.

Idea: progress writes **only** to `IO.ErrOut`. This reinforces
byob-iostreams.3 (data to Out, chatter to ErrOut) and byob-output.1
(TTY-adaptive output goes to the adaptive side). Data — the thing
a user might pipe — stays on Out, uncluttered. Chatter + progress
share ErrOut; the byob-logging.4 "quiet by default" posture keeps logs
out of the way unless asked.

Rule of thumb: if removing a print would change what a pipe
consumer sees, that print belongs to Out. Progress indicators never
qualify — their entire job is ephemeral status.

Tradeoffs: none worth noting. This is a corollary of byob-iostreams.3
more than a new decision.

title: Prompter as a narrow consumer interface
description:
Problem: a wide prompter interface (`AskOne`, `AskMany`, 20 options
per call) couples every command to a specific library's question
shape. When the library changes — or the implementation swaps for
tests — the blast radius is large.

Idea: five methods is the minimum that covers a real CLI. Each
takes `context.Context` as its first argument so prompts inherit
the caller's deadline and cancellation — a command with a deadline
should be able to abandon a hung prompt instead of waiting on
stdin forever:

```go
type Prompter interface {
    Confirm(ctx context.Context, msg string, def bool) (bool, error)
    Input(ctx context.Context, msg, def string) (string, error)
    Password(ctx context.Context, msg string) (string, error)
    Select(ctx context.Context, msg string, options []string) (int, error)
    MultiSelect(ctx context.Context, msg string, options []string) ([]int, error)
}
```

Per byob-interfaces.1, the interface lives in `pkg/cmd/prompt/` (or closer
to the consumer) and concrete impls (live, stub) satisfy it
structurally. No library type leaks into the consumer.

Tradeoffs: five methods won't cover every fancy UX (autocomplete
pickers, path completers, multi-line editors). When you need one,
add a dedicated method — don't stretch `Input` to do it. The ctx
parameter is uniform across all methods even though most callers
will pass the command's root ctx untouched — the consistency
matters more than per-method ergonomics.

title: Staffing / FTE
description: Authorized positions, Budget Book p247-252 ('Regular, At-Will or Limited Duration'). Pairs with the ACFR's ten-year FTE-by-function table.

title: CIP project explorer
description: Filter/search projects by program, fund and year. CIP p40-41 program summaries and per-project funding tables are the one place table extraction works WELL (52% recall overall but these pages extract cleanly). Same two filters as the CIP node work: appropriated years only, new appropriations only.

title: Line-item revenue trends
description: Every revenue row on p127-140 already carries four fiscal-year columns (FY23-24 actual, FY24-25 revised, FY25-26 and FY26-27 budget), so each line is a 4-point series with NO extra extraction once E7's GF revenue mapping exists.

title: Fund explorer
description: Sources/uses and reserves per fund with the restricted flag made explicit -- the thing the Sankey can only gesture at. Source: Fund Balances by Major/Non-Major Fund, Budget Book p68-75, plus funds.yaml.

title: Department pages
description: The view most residents actually want: what does Police cost and who pays for it. Source: the per-department pages (Expenditures by Category by division, Department Funding Sources by fund) plus performance measures (e.g. p48).

title: E8 Further projections
description: The fact store is the product; the Sankey is one projection. Each of these is independent -- pick by interest.

title: CIP funds as nodes: appropriated years, new appropriations only
description:
The CIP is NOT double-counted inside the operating budget -- verified arithmetically to the dollar:
  transfers OUT (p66-67)          59,612,734
  transfers IN  (p66-67)        - 21,525,997
  gap to CIP funds                38,086,737
  + CIP grants direct (p222)    +  8,997,886
                                  47,084,623  == stated FY2025-26 CIP appropriation (p222)

So the citywide schedule already contains the CIP as a $38.1M transfer-out that goes NOWHERE unless CIP funds are modelled as nodes. The diagram does not balance without them. Bridge table is p222 ('CIP Project Fund (Receiving) / Operating Fund (Transferring)'); dedicated CIP funds are listed at p253-254.

TWO HARD FILTERS: only FY2025-26 and FY2026-27 are appropriated (the CIP's tables run to FY2030-45, which is planning intent, not budget); and the CIP's $141.3M two-year figure includes $35.2M of carry-forward (p211), so only the $106.1M of NEW appropriations is FY26+FY27 money.

title: ACFR as a separate function-axis view (scope: governmental-net)
description:
NOT a sibling in a year toggle -- it is structurally a different chart. The ACFR has three fund columns (General, Low Income Housing, Other Governmental), an expenditure axis by FUNCTION (Police, Fire, Public Works) rather than object category, ISF eliminated, and $55,286,695 of fiduciary custodial payments that are not the city's money (declare fiduciary out of scope with a note on the page). There is no object-category breakdown anywhere in the ACFR.

The UI must never offer a year-toggle between datasets of different scope. Label it as a different accounting basis.

title: All-funds toggle rendering tiers 0-3 with the constraint tier
description:
The General Fund is $144.7M of $254.1M (57%); the other 43% is water/sewer/airport ratepayer money, gas tax, impact fees, assessments and grants, almost all legally restricted. A single all-funds Sankey makes the visual claim that money pools and is then allocated, which is false for that 43% -- water rates cannot pay for police. So all-funds is a deliberate second click, and restricted funds render as a visually separated, labelled band driven by funds.yaml constraint_tier, not merely a different hue.

Also surface the Internal Service Fund double-count: ISF expenditures are $25,077,367 whose $18,969,834 of revenue is charges to other city departments, already counted inside those departments. The ACFR eliminates ISF activity; the Budget Book does not.
notes: 2026-08-18 THIS, NOT fisc-gxa.2, IS WHERE AN EARLY-RENDER ARGUMENT BELONGS. Landing plan wanted a visible milestone between the coverage lanes. fisc-gxa.2 cannot supply one after fisc-5gk.1 alone (see its note of the same date: within the General Fund tier 3 is a single node). But pp.131-140 print 'REVENUE SOURCES BY FUNDS / OTHER FUNDS' fund by fund, which does make a real tier-3 axis: data/funds.yaml already carries 112 numbered funds with constraint_tier, and fact.Fact.Fund int already exists (internal/fact/fact.go:72). So the all-funds tiers 0,1,2,3 view this bead describes becomes genuinely renderable once fisc-5gk.1 lands, without waiting for departments. If that ordering is wanted, argue it here and record the reasoning.

title: fisc reanchor --accept
description: Bulk-rewrites integrity hashes after a reviewed extraction change. This is what converts an xberg bump from 're-anchor N rules blind' into one commit with a readable diff.

title: Schema-validation test over every committed data file
description: Every file under data/ validates against its schema_version. Runs in CI over the whole tree.

title: Determinism test: re-extract a fixture, assert byte-identical
description: Determinism is already confirmed empirically (ACFR run 3x, identical hashes); this test keeps it true. Note doc.tables order was stable across three single-machine runs but is not documented as stable across core counts -- the explicit sort in the serializer is what removes that dependency.
notes:
2026-08-22 THIS BEAD IS WRITTEN AGAINST THE RETIRED EXTRACTOR and needs
re-framing before it is actionable. Flagged while planning the backlog waves.

The description says "doc.tables order was stable across three single-machine
runs but is not documented as stable across core counts -- the explicit sort in
the serializer is what removes that dependency". There is no doc.tables. The
poppler migration (fisc-yqv) removed the table substrate entirely; see the
poppler-not-xberg memory: "There is NO table substrate and no Substrate enum".
So the specific determinism hazard this bead names no longer exists.

WHAT REPLACES IT is not nothing -- determinism is still a real property with
real hazards, just different ones. docs/agents/conventions.md states them:
"words sorted by position rather than by the tool's emission order, canonical
JSON with sorted keys, bboxes rounded to 2dp, atomic writes". Each is a thing
that could regress.

THE HARD CONSTRAINT this bead has to design around, and it is why the answer is
probably not a Go test: conventions.md says "Go tests never require Python, the
source PDFs, or the network", and re-extracting a fixture requires poppler AND
a PDF from LFS. So this cannot be `go test`. Candidates:

- a job in the monthly --full workflow (fisc-v87), which already takes the LFS
  cost and already has the PDFs checked out;
- a `make` target run by hand at extractor-bump time, which is when the
  property is actually at risk;
- a pure-Go test over the SERIALIZER only, feeding it synthetic word lists and
  asserting sorted output -- which needs no PDF and would catch the sort
  regression, though not a poppler-side change.

The third is the only one that fits the Go-tests-are-hermetic rule, and it
tests our half rather than poppler's. Decide which of the three (or which
combination) before writing anything.

Also worth stating: determinism was confirmed empirically at extraction time
(ACFR run 3x, identical hashes) and artifacts-match-manifest already guards the
COMMITTED artifacts against drift on every fisc verify run. So the gap is
narrower than the bead implies -- it is specifically "a re-extraction produces
the same bytes", which only matters at extractor-bump time.

title: internal/check/fixture_test.go: testDocs's doc comment now sits on inlinePageDoc
description:
inlinePageDoc was inserted immediately after testDocss doc comment
(internal/check/fixture_test.go:208), so that comment now documents the wrong
function and testDocs has none. Mechanical; found by /code-review 2026-08-24.

title: A wrapped_labels fragment sharing the leading gap with column headers is neither declarable nor omittable
description:
internal/mapping/resolve.go:562, in checkGap's leading-gap branch: a declared
wrapped_labels fragment is admitted only when the TRIMMED GAP EQUALS THE
FRAGMENT EXACTLY.

The branch's own comment says the leading gap is where a part's column headers
live -- which is why that branch exists at all, and why it refuses digits rather
than refusing text. So a page that wraps a label INTO that gap, beside the
headers, produces a gap that is header text plus the fragment, matches neither
the exact-equality test nor OmittedRows (which is about rows the DOCUMENT does
not print, a different claim), and the part cannot be expressed.

NOT REACHED BY ANY COMMITTED PAGE, which is why this is P3 rather than a
blocker. pp.127-140's straddle tail parts anchor on "FY 2026-27\n" and their
leading gap is empty; pp.167-170's wrapped labels (fisc-0cs) land BETWEEN rows,
not before the first one, and that path is the one 664d638 covers.

Worth filing rather than discovering: the schedules still unmapped are the ones
most likely to hit it. CIP pp.29-40 wrap project names and the ACFR wraps
account descriptions, and a fragment that cannot be declared fails closed --
correct, but with an error message that tells the author to declare something
the parser will then refuse.

Found by /code-review of the fisc-5gk.1 lane, 2026-08-24.
acceptance_criteria: a wrapped fragment in the leading gap alongside column headers is either declarable or refused with an error that says it cannot be declared here and why; a test carries the page shape

title: beginning + change - ending == 0 is asserted by nothing
description:
Found and MEASURED while closing fisc-4er, 2026-08-24.

THE CLAIM: for every (fund group, fiscal year) the spine publishes,

    fund-balance/beginning + fund-balance/change == fund-balance/ending

VERIFIED over facts/facts.jsonl restricted to all-funds-gross: it holds at zero
in all twelve cells. Three published cells per year per group, 36 facts, and
the identity between them is asserted by nothing today.

WHY IT IS NOT fisc-4er, which was closed as already satisfied.
TestPublishedSpineBalancesPerFundGroup (internal/mapping/mappings_test.go:253)
covers the RESIDUAL identity -- revenue + transfers in - expenditure -
transfers out - reserve increase == change -- and pins both sides to the
printed TOTAL SOURCES / TOTAL USES. It says nothing about beginning and ending,
which are two more printed cells on the same rows of pp.66-67.

SIZE: small. Both sides are in the fact store; this is a check or a test, not a
mapping change. Deliberately kept out of fisc-4er's scope because folding a
second claim into one assertion makes a failure ambiguous about which claim
broke.

title: A rollup may cover rules of different kinds or scopes, and nothing compares them
description:
Found reviewing the fisc-7fe fix, 2026-08-24, and deliberately NOT fixed there
because unlike the basis case it is not obviously wrong.

WHAT IS NOW GUARDED. CheckRollup compares the covered rules' bearer-part
columns element by element, on the EFFECTIVE basis (fisc-7fe, plus the basis
half found in review). validateRollups compares Units and Parts[0].Columns.

WHAT IS NOT. Rule.Kind and Rule.Scope are compared by nothing. A rollup may
cover an expenditure rule and a revenue rule, or a rule at all-funds-gross and
one at expenditure-by-department, and the sum is reported as a clean tie if the
figures happen to add up.

WHY IT IS NOT OBVIOUSLY A BUG, which is the reason this is its own bead rather
than a line in that fix. p140's "Total Sources" is literally revenue plus
transfers in -- a printed total over two kinds. It is declared unassertable
today (fisc-wev), so nothing exercises the case, but it is the document's own
evidence that a mixed-kind rollup can be a real printed line rather than an
author error. Refusing it outright would be choosing a rule the corpus has not
yet asked for.

SCOPE IS DIFFERENT FROM KIND and may deserve the opposite answer. A rollup
summing a detail-scope total into a spine-scope one is the fisc-u2v doubling
mechanism at the rollup level: the two are the same money, so a tie there means
the arithmetic worked and the claim is still wrong.

WHAT TO DECIDE: whether scope must match (probably yes, and refusable at parse
time -- it needs no pages), and whether kind must match or must merely be
DECLARED when it varies, so a mixed-kind rollup is a statement rather than an
accident.

title: A wrapped label before a part's first mapped row cannot be declared
description:
internal/mapping/resolve.go:519-539. WrappedLabels is consumed in two places inside labelledValues: checkGap admits a gap whose trimmed text is declared, and a trailing fragment after the last row is admitted the same way. Both mark the declaration USED, and an entry the page never used is refused (resolve.go:532) -- which is the right shape, because a stale declaration is a claim about the page that has stopped being true.

THE GAP THIS LEAVES. checkGap's i == 0 case admits the text before the FIRST mapped row without consulting WrappedLabels and without marking anything used. So a wrapped label landing there cannot be declared at all: declaring it fails with 'is declared but does not appear between this part's rows', and not declaring it is accepted silently. The one shape where a fragment is invisible either way.

NOT TRIGGERED BY pp.167-170 AS MAPPED. All four wrapping division labels there put their HEAD in the section anchor and their tail between two rows, so every tail is declarable. It is reachable by anchoring differently on the same page: section 'Innovation &' leaves 'Economic' in the i == 0 gap.

ALSO IN THE SAME FIELD, and this is fisc-ekj: WrappedLabels is read only by labelledValues, so a declaration on a labels_from part is neither used nor stale-checked. The two are one fix -- decide where the field is consulted and make every declaration on every part either used or refused.

FIX SHAPE: have the i == 0 gap consult WrappedLabels and mark it used, keeping the current permissiveness for undeclared leading whitespace-plus-text only if there is a reason for it. Note that tightening it may make an existing part fail; check the spine's parts before landing.

Found by /code-review of the fisc-5gk.2 landing, 2026-08-23.
close_reason: Landed in 664d638 as one fix, per fisc-2jk's own framing. ekj refused at parse time on a labels_from part, with the bead's recorded p67 measurement re-run against the fix; 2jk's i==0 gap now consults WrappedLabels and marks it used, keeping the column-header permissiveness for a stated reason. Both proven red first.

title: A dangling $ late in a block is reported against the block's FIRST row
description:
internal/mapping/resolve.go:497. labelledValues calls

    dropCurrencyMarks(tokens(blk.Text[after:], blk.Start+after))

on the WHOLE REMAINDER OF THE BLOCK, for every row, and only afterwards truncates with `toks = toks[:ncols]`.

dropCurrencyMarks scans everything it is given, so a detached '$' sitting on the LAST row of a block makes the FIRST row's call return the error, and the message names that first row:

    row "Wages & Benefits": "$" is a currency mark with no figure after it

The reader then goes and looks at a row that is perfectly fine. The check itself is right -- a bare '$' must never be silently dropped, which is what dde657b landed it for -- and only the attribution is wrong.

FIX: truncate before checking, or pass dropCurrencyMarks the row's own span. Careful: the truncation currently depends on the currency marks having been removed first (a '$' would otherwise occupy one of the ncols slots), so the two cannot simply be swapped -- the row's span has to be found some other way, e.g. by dropping marks lazily until ncols figures are in hand.

TEST: a block whose last row carries a detached '$' must name the LAST row. A test with a single row, or with the mark on the first row, passes either way.

Found by /code-review of the fisc-o15 landing, 2026-08-23, and verified against the source.

title: CheckRollup panics on a rollup with no covers instead of erroring
description:
internal/mapping/resolve.go:988 and :977 index `rules[0]` with no length check. `coveredRules` returns an empty slice for a Rollup whose `covers` is empty, so CheckRollup panics with index out of range rather than returning an error.

WHY IT IS UNREACHABLE TODAY, and why that is not the same as safe. Two things keep it so, and neither is CheckRollup's own: parse.go refuses a rollup that declares neither covers nor unassertable, and pkg/cmd/build/report.go:194-199 skips CheckRollup entirely for an unassertable one. CheckRollup is EXPORTED, so a second caller -- a verify-side structural sweep (fisc-1wr.5) is the obvious one -- reintroduces the panic by doing nothing wrong.

This is the same class as the panic fisc-3bl already fixed in this function (column width taken from Parts[0] where the totals came from a later part). That one was reachable; this one is one caller away.

FIX: return a ResolveError naming the rollup when len(rules) == 0, before either index.

Found by /code-review of the fisc-o15 landing, 2026-08-23, and verified against the source.
close_reason: Landed in a3adb0e. fisc-7fe fixed element-wise on the EFFECTIVE basis (the Column.Basis override half was found in review of the fix); fisc-7a6 fixed at both sites, its premise corrected on the bead first; fisc-t9h guarded before both rules[0] indexes. Each test proven red against the prior code. Kind/scope left uncompared and filed separately.

title: [bug] registry.Alias's doc comment carries two concatenated intros, and the stale half names the wrong field
description:
internal/registry/registry.go:92. The Alias doc comment has two intros joined from a bad merge. The surviving-but-stale half attributes the evidence role to Note -- which is unvalidated and read by nothing -- rather than to Rationale, which validateFundAlias actually enforces.

Not a behaviour bug: the code is right and the comment is wrong. It matters because the comment is the thing a rule author reads when deciding where to put the page citation for an alias, and it currently points them at the field that will not be checked. That is the same shape as a declaration that cannot fail.

Found by /code-review over the fisc-3bl work, 2026-08-23. Not fixed there because it is in a package that lane does not touch and bundling it would have hidden it.

title: Spine rule merge: a kind filter on the total_row declaration, five rules to three
description:
This is the work fisc-uli was ORIGINALLY written for, separated from Row.Kind
because fisc-uli's own 2026-08-21 correction shows the two want opposite things
from CheckTotals.

THE SAVING. The p66-67 spine needs five rules where three would do, because Kind
is per-Rule and the transfers and fund-balance rows share a printed block with
the expenditure rows. Each rule re-declares the whole block with skip: true on
the rows it does not own -- correct and fail-closed, but verbose and easy to get
wrong in review. mappings/livermore-budget-fy2026-2027.yaml carries five rules
over ten parts for this reason.

WHY IT IS NOT PART OF Row.Kind. Merging spine-revenues (total_row
"TOTAL REVENUES:") with spine-transfers-in gives a rule whose printed total
covers ONLY the revenue rows, so the merged rule needs CheckTotals to sum BY
KIND. But fisc-5gk.1's eleven mixed fund blocks on pp.131-140 print a total that
covers BOTH kinds, and there CheckTotals' existing kind-BLINDNESS is exactly
what is wanted. A globally kind-aware CheckTotals makes p131's Airport block
stop tying to Total Airport (which includes Transfers In 3,247,000) and fails
all eleven.

THE RESOLUTION fisc-uli records: the kind filter belongs on the total_row
DECLARATION, not on CheckTotals globally. A total row is the thing that knows
which rows it covers, and saying so is a claim the rule author makes and review
can check -- the same shape as Column.Basis overriding Rule.Basis on the COLUMN,
the thing that knows.

SO THIS BEAD IS: a kind filter on the total_row declaration, plus the spine rule
merge it enables. Row.Kind itself is fisc-uli and lands with CheckTotals
untouched.

NOT URGENT. Nothing is blocked on it -- the five-rule spine is correct today and
the eleven mixed blocks work with kind-blind CheckTotals. This is a readability
and review-surface saving, which is what fisc-uli was before the fisc-u2v design
pass promoted its other half.

THE PROOF IT IS SAFE, when done: facts.jsonl byte-identical. A rule merge that
moves a fact has changed a published claim, because rule_id is in fact.MakeID's
tuple -- so this cannot be done without re-anchoring, and that cost belongs in
the estimate.
acceptance_criteria: a total_row declaration may name the kinds it covers; the spine's five rules become three; the eleven mixed fund blocks on pp.131-140 still tie under kind-blind totals; the facts.jsonl diff is exactly the rule_id changes the merge forces and nothing else

title: Cross-part column_headers agreement will need relaxing for a page with two grids
description:
fisc-yqv.2's parser requires every part reading a page of a document to declare
the SAME column_headers, and requires them all to opt in or none to. It catches a
real failure: the published spine writes one page's header list out five times,
and a drifted copy would build a different grid for the same page in one rule
than in another, with both reads still tying against their own printed totals.

But a page that prints two schedules side by side with different grids is not a
defect, and the check refuses one. No page in this corpus does yet; the CIP is
the obvious candidate. When one appears, the grouping key has to become finer
than (doc_id, page) -- probably the header line itself -- without losing the
drifted-copy catch.

See checkColumnGrids in internal/mapping/parse.go.
acceptance_criteria: a page printing two schedules with different grids can be mapped; the drifted-copy failure the check exists for is still caught

title: column_headers_ordinal, when a page forces it
description:
fisc-yqv.2's design specified column_headers_ordinal, mirroring section_ordinal.
It was dropped, measured: the full ordered header sequence occurs exactly ONCE
page-wide on 66, 67, 127, 128-140, 167, 168, 169, 170, CIP 40 and CIP 29, with
zero unconsumed words right of the first match on every one.

An ordered multi-entry sequence is a far stronger anchor than the single
substrings section_ordinal exists for ("REVENUES:" genuinely occurs twice on p66).
Shipping five validation branches and a selection branch no fixture could reach,
inside the guard everything else now trusts, was the worse trade.

Today an ambiguous header line is a refusal that names the candidate lines and
hints that no ordinal exists. Add the key when a real page forces it, WITH that
page as the fixture.
acceptance_criteria: the page that forces it is named, is committed as a fixture, and the ordinal's selection and validation branches are exercised by it

title: data/sources.yaml has two readers; pkg/cmd/export keeps its own
description:
internal/registry.LoadSources (fisc-1wr.5, lane A4) is now the strict, schema-gated reader of the whole source registry: it declares every key, so a key added to the file without being declared is a load failure rather than a silently dropped claim. pkg/cmd/export/data.go still carries sourceRegistry, a narrow non-validating view of four fields (id, title, publisher, url) used to build the site's citation targets.

Consolidating means loadDocs calls registry.LoadSources and maps Source -> export.Doc, which deletes a yaml.Unmarshal and a struct. It was deliberately NOT done in A4 for one reason worth recording: LoadSources validates sha256 and bytes, so `fisc export` would start refusing to run over a registry entry that carries no hash -- a behaviour change to the publishing path, in a lane about verification. pkg/cmd/export/export_test.go's fakeRepo would also have to grow file/bytes/sha256 fields it does not read.

Do it as its own change, with a decision about whether export should require the integrity fields (probably yes: a source the site cites with no recorded hash is a citation nobody can check).

title: Permanent Funds are a seventh fund type with no spine column
description: data/funds.yaml has 7 type values; the pp.66-67 schedule prints 6 columns. type: permanent covers 2 funds (470 Doolan Canyon Preserve Endowment, 471 Doolan Canyon Open Space) and no column on the citywide spine accounts for them. Column totals tie regardless because the check is per-column, not a partition check over all 112 funds -- so nothing currently notices. Establish where those funds land in the citywide roll-up before any check claims the spine partitions the fund list.
notes:
2026-08-18 FIRST PUBLISHED MONEY for the seventh fund type: Budget Book p76 prints a 'Permanent Funds' DESTINATION section -- 'Transfer From Open Space to Doolan Canyon Preserve Endow', 19,533 in FY2023-24 and '-' in the other three columns. So the schedule that has no Permanent column on pp.66-67 does carry a Permanent row one page group over, and p76's grand total spans a fund group the spine does not print. It nets to zero for FY2026 and FY2027, which is why p76's budget columns still tie to the spine exactly; it would NOT tie if the historical columns were ever mapped. Found reconciling p76 (fisc-5gk.3).
2026-08-21 NOW EVIDENCED RATHER THAN SUSPECTED, from the fisc-u2v design pass.
Budget Book p134 prints the Permanent Funds section as `Doolan Canyon Preserve
Endow` (data/funds.yaml fund 470, name truncated on the page -- see fisc-8dz).
It is TRANSFERS-ONLY and ZERO in both budget years, FY2025-26 and FY2026-27.

That matters twice over.

FIRST, it is why fisc-u2v's revenue-detail-ties-to-spine can be an exact
identity. pp.127-140 reproduce the whole revenue side of pp.66-67 to the cent
for all six fund groups -- and Permanent Funds, which pp.66-67 have no column
for, is the one section that could have broken the tie. It does not, because it
is zero in exactly the years reconciled.

SECOND, it makes the seventh-fund-type problem DEFERRABLE ON EVIDENCE rather
than merely unaddressed: nothing is being dropped from a published figure today.
The condition under which that stops being true is stated and checkable -- the
section becoming non-zero in a budget column.

So the reconciliation check should assert permanent is zero in the reconciled
years AND non-zero in FY2024, the way transfers_p76_test.go pins the residual:
the check then reddens if the page stops evidencing this bead, instead of
silently absorbing the change. Do not write it as a blanket exclusion of the
permanent fund type.

title: Gann appropriations limit
description: Budget Book p38, 'Constitutional Spending Limits'. Small, and genuinely interesting: the limit vs actual appropriations.
